articles.title: Tall athletes can't stretch their legs in container beds at Asian Games, official says
articles.summary: South Korea's delegation slams the wooden containers housing its athletes at the Asian Games in Nagoya city.

blocks.text: Wooden container huts meant for thousands of athletes have become the subject of heated criticism ahead of the opening of Japan's Asian Games on Saturday.
Jung Jae-yong, vice-president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP news agency the accommodation was the "worst it has ever been".
"Athletes who are over two metres (6ft 7in) tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It's unreasonable."

The Games, held in the city of Nagoya and wider Aichi prefecture, have faced weeks of concern about a potential shortage of beds. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are attending - exceeding the initial 15,000 expected.
The containers, which will be housing around 2,000 of the guests and are designed to be reused as disaster evacuation facilities, have been beset by complaints.
A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me."
Athletes were also briefly evacuated from the containers as record rainfall lashed Nagoya last week and caused widespread flooding. Water leakage was reported in some of the competition venues too.
Jung, the basketball official, told AFP that concerns over accommodation were shared by representatives from the other countries at the Games.
Indian authorities have built replicas of the huts to get their athletes used to living in them.
Accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters the hosts were "fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns voiced by the athlete delegations".
They were "taking concrete steps to improve the environment for the athletes", he said.
Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is usually a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors.
Beyond the container huts, between 4,000 and 5,000 participants will be staying on an Italian cruise ship which docked in Nagoya on Tuesday. The rest of the attendees will stay in hotels.
Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials had been expected to attend the Games.
But in mid-August the Olympic Council of Asia said the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included.

Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, previously said authorities had set aside a budget for 15,000 people and had "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the additional athletes.
"There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements."

But last month, organisers and the Olympic Council of Asia said all "17,000-plus" athletes and officials who had registered before the deadline in July have been provided with "Games-appropriate accommodation".
"The final preparations are all on track and progressing smoothly ahead of what promises to be the most spectacular Asian Games held for generations," their statement read.
Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino told AFP that while all the country's athletes have secured a bed, some officials and coaches were staying in "different hotels and Airbnb".
Though basketball and football matches have already started, the Asian Games officially begin on Saturday and will end on 4 October.

articles.title: Ex-SC justices: No violation of due process if 16 votes are changed
articles.summary: Former Supreme Court (SC) chief justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno, and Adolfo Azcuna said Wednesday that there is no violation of due process if ever the Senate, acting as impeachment court,…

blocks.text: Former Supreme Court (SC) chief justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno, and Adolfo Azcuna said Wednesday that there is no violation of due process if ever the Senate, acting as impeachment court, decides to change the voting threshold of 16 to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

Senator-judge Francis Kiko Pangilinan asked the three amici curiae, or "friends of the court," whether they think there will be a violation of due process if the voting threshold is changed while the trial is already ongoing.

"There has been some commentary that the threshold vote ay changing the rules. Therefore, the due process requirement of the respondent and even the prosecution, when you change the rules in the middle of the proceedings, maapektuhan yung due process clause. Kasi dapat hindi binabago habang nagkakaroon ng paglilitis. Could you care to comment?" Pangilinan asked.

(There has been some commentary that [revising] the threshold vote is changing the rules. Therefore, the due process requirement of the respondent and even the prosecution—when you change the rules in the middle of the proceedings, the due process clause gets affected. Because rules shouldn't be changed while a trial is ongoing. Could you care to comment?)
Panganiban said that there is no violation as the voting has yet to commence.

"Wala pa pong paglabag, sapagkat hindi pa kayo bumuboto. In other words, it hasn't been implemented. Wala pa po. Hindi pa ini-implement. Kaya tuwing yung ginagawa niyo nga, you are anticipating the issue, the problem. So commendably, you are doing this meeting so that you cannot be accused of grave abuse of discretion kung sakaling dumating 'yun," he said.

(There is no violation yet, because you haven't voted yet. In other words, it hasn't been implemented. Not yet. It hasn't been implemented. So with what you are doing, you are anticipating the issue, the problem. So commendably, you are holding this meeting so that you cannot be accused of grave abuse of discretion should that time come.)
"Maaaring magpalit at isip niyo ngayon, pagkat hindi pa nangyayari, hindi pa kayo nagbobotohan. Kaya there is no grave abuse of discretion, in my humble opinion, as of now," he added.
(You may change your mind right now, because it hasn't happened yet—you haven't taken a vote yet. That's why there is no grave abuse of discretion, in my humble opinion, as of now.)
Pangilinan repeated the question to the two other former SC justices.

"Our presiding officer has ruled that it is 16. Now, if we reconsider that ruling and decide as a court that it is lower than 16, or if we decide that it is 16, walang problema. Pero if we decide it's lower, is it a denial of the respondent's right to due process that the rules were changed in the middle of the proceedings?" he asked.

(Our presiding officer has ruled that it is 16. Now, if we reconsider that ruling and decide as a court that it is lower than 16, or if we decide that it is 16, there is no problem. But if we decide it's lower, is it a denial of the respondent's right to due process that the rules were changed in the middle of the proceedings?)
Puno noted that the impeachment court is currently discussing the rule.

"It's a vague question when you say changing the rule. Wala pa naman talagang rule. Tsaka kung ang ginagawa po ay tinatalakay kung ano talaga yung meaning nung particular rule na 'yun, ay hindi po changing the rule 'yun. Tinatama lang yung dapat maging interpretasyon nung rule, lalong lalo na yung isang rule na napakaraming reasonable interpretations," he said.

(It's a vague question when you say changing the rule. There isn't really a settled rule yet. Besides, if what is being done is discussing the actual meaning of that particular rule, that isn't changing the rule. It's simply correcting what the proper interpretation of the rule should be, especially for a rule that has so many reasonable interpretations.)

"Dapat yung aakyat sa Supreme Court must demonstrate an injury. Papaano ide-demonstrate yung injury na 'yun kung wala pang final interpretation yung Senate, wala pang applicability ito," Puno added. "Baka yung bagong interpretasyon ay makinabang pa yung magre-raise ng constitutional issue. Palagay ko ay hindi tatanggapin ng Korte Suprema itong issue na ito sa panahon na ito. It's a matter of perfect timing."

(Whoever goes to the Supreme Court must demonstrate an injury. How can that injury be demonstrated if the Senate hasn't rendered a final interpretation yet, and when there is no applicability so far? The party raising the constitutional issue might even benefit from the new interpretation. I believe the Supreme Court will not entertain this issue at this time. It's a matter of perfect timing.)
Meanwhile, Azcuna echoed the sentiments of his colleagues.

"Because the question of the interpretation of the 2/3 is a procedural matter. And procedural matters can be retroactive. There is no vested right to a procedure. So the rule is if it's procedural, it can be applied to pending cases," he said.

"So even if the trial has already started and you change the interpretation of the presiding officer, I think there is no violation of due process. There's no vested right that has been violated because all these matters are procedural," Azcuna added.

After his election as presiding officer, Senator Francis Escudero stressed that the 1987 Constitution provides that no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate or 16 votes.
Escudero also confirmed that his statement constituted a formal ruling of the impeachment court, which is subject to any legal remedies available to the parties.
Meanwhile, four of the current 24 senator-judges of the vice president's trial are either detained for plunder cases or remain in hiding. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Revealed: the UK towns with the fewest jobs for young people
articles.summary:
Rotherham has 46 online vacancies for every 1,000 young people but there are 288 in Cotswold district council area

Young people in Rotherham face a local jobs market with the fewest suitable…

blocks.text: Young people in Rotherham face a local jobs market with the fewest suitable opportunities in Britain, according to a report that warns stark regional divisions are fuelling a crisis in youth work.

As ministers push to combat rising youth unemployment, the analysis from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) showed young people faced a tougher challenge in some parts of the country to find work than in others.

Publishing a new “local youth opportunity index” to track job vacancies across Britain, it said there was a sixfold gap in jobs in the South Yorkshire town compared with the more affluent Cotswolds, where there are fewer young adults but more opportunities.

Whereas Rotherham has 46 online job vacancies for every 1,000 young people, there are 288 in the area covered by Cotswold district council. Highlighting deep regional divisions, the report found nine of the 10 best areas for youth job opportunities are in the south of England.

Places with job openings relative to the local youth population below the national average of 109, include East Renfrewshire in Scotland, Newcastle-under-Lyme in Staffordshire, and Broxtowe in Nottinghamshire. Cities including Sheffield, Coventry and Cardiff also ranked near the bottom of the list for youth employment opportunities.
Places with the most opportunities included Woking in Surrey, Gloucester, Cherwell in Oxfordshire, and Warrington in the north-west of England.

The analysis comes as ministers await recommendations from a highly anticipated report by Alan Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness. The former Labour health secretary, who is expected to publish his findings next month before the autumn budget, has called for a policy overhaul involving education, welfare and employment support.

Britain’s young adults are bearing the brunt of a rise in unemployment, with the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neet) surpassing 1 million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade.
Representing as many as one in eight young people, the rate has swelled at a significantly faster rate than in other countries amid a sharp rise in mental ill health and a tough jobs market.

The IPPR said its report showed that becoming Neet was not simply a question of an individual’s qualifications or willingness to look for work. It urged ministers to prioritise overhauling the apprenticeship system and to create a new “work start” programme that would fund youth jobs in areas with too few entry-level opportunities. It also called for a new “youth allowance” that would replace different rates of universal credit benefits based on work capability.
after newsletter promotion

Responding to the IPPR report, David Blunkett, the former Labour education secretary, said he had first-hand experience of the challenges facing young people from growing up on a Sheffield council estate and leaving school at 16 with no qualifications.

“Young people have an immense amount to give. With national ambition, local leadership and the willingness to invest, we can ensure that birthplace does not determine a young person’s future,” he said.

“We can renew the promise that should lie at the heart of any decent society: that no young person will be discarded, that the door to opportunity will remain open and that everyone will have the chance to build a life of purpose.”
A government spokesperson said: “Where you’re from should never determine where you end up in life.

“The Milburn review will lay the foundation for further youth employment reform, but thanks to our £2.5bn investment, we are already taking action, including reprioritising apprenticeships for young people and rolling out youth hubs to every community, helping us create one million work and training opportunities.
“We are also supporting businesses to back young talent by offering hiring incentives worth up to £8,000 and continuing the national insurance exemptions for under 21s and apprentices under 25.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Sept. 16: Friends of the court
articles.summary: Impeachment has been tagged as a numbers game. Today, the Senate impeachment court made that literal, pausing its regular programming to hear four legal luminaries weigh in on two questions: Who…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Impeachment has been tagged as a numbers game. Today, the Senate impeachment court made that literal, pausing its regular programming to hear four legal luminaries weigh in on two questions: Who counts, and how many?

On Wednesday, September 16, retired Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno and retired Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna appeared in person as amici curiae, or friends of the court. Retired Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr., who recently underwent a medical procedure, sent his views in a written memorandum.
The amici were asked to help resolve three issues raised in Sen. Erwin Tulfo's appeal of Escudero's ruling that 16 of 24 senators are needed to convict.
The first is whether "all the members of the Senate" in the Constitution's two-thirds rule means all 24 senators or only those legally and physically able to take part.

The second is whether Avelino v. Cuenco, a 1949 Supreme Court ruling that excluded a senator beyond the chamber's reach from a quorum count, applies to senators who are detained, abroad, suspended, or whose whereabouts are unknown.
The third is whether a senator-judge who did not attend or substantially take part in the trial may still vote on the verdict.
Here's a summary of where the retired justices stood on each question.
Question 1: In voting to convict, is it a fixed 16 or a moving number?

On the central question, the amici split three to one. Davide, Panganiban and Puno said the two-thirds should be based on senators who can actually take part and hear witnesses in the proceedings. Azcuna held that all 24 senators must be counted unless a seat becomes permanently vacant.
Davide: Count only those qualified to vote

Davide, a delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention and a member of the 1986 Constitutional Commission, wrote that the framers never argued over the phrase. "There was no debate on this subject during the deliberations in both the 1973 Convention and the Constitutional Commission of 1986," he said.
The framers assumed "members" meant senators able to perform their duties, he said, and any other reading would "tolerate an absurdity, and perpetuate an injustice."

Davide listed senators he said should be left out of the count: those who resigned or were expelled, those with serious mental or physical incapacity, those outside the country, in hiding, or whose whereabouts are unknown, and those under legal restraint, including senators charged with plunder or graft.
"Clearly then, the basis of computing the two-thirds must be the number of senators who are qualified to vote, not the 24 in the present Senate," he wrote.
Panganiban: 16 holds only 'in the abstract' and court must act in favor of justice
In his opening remarks, Panganiban granted that a literal reading yields 16 votes. But "reality ... changes the denominator in mathematics," he said.
"We must look at the intent and the purpose of constitutional provisions, the circumstances in which they operate and the goals they seek to achieve."

Panganiban reminded senators they are "not jurists" and are called upon "to decide as lawmakers." He urged them to read the Constitution with the common sense of the people, guided by "two fundamental standards, namely truth and fairness."
"You are tasked with a constitutional duty that cannot always be reduced to abstract arithmetic. Neither can such duty be performed in the shadows of absence nor from legal impediments," he said.

Sen. Erwin Tulfo later, during his turn for questions, posed a hypothetical to the amici. He posed a scenario where several senators are unable to attend through no choice of their own, whether because of illness, detention, or other circumstances, leaving too few to reach 16 votes.
He asked whether the purpose of impeachment still supports "maintaining a fixed 16-vote requirement even if the Senate cannot realistically exercise its power to decide the case."
"You have given an example of why 16 should not be fixed," Panganiban said. If only 16 senators remained, he said, a fixed threshold would demand a unanimous vote.
"That means that all 16 must vote unanimously. I don't think so," he said. "Otherwise, you'll have to immobilize the Senate as a source of justice for our people."

"Legalities do not matter very much because our people are not lawyers. They're not jurists. They are not used to objecting to leading questions or misleading questions. They're not used to technicalities. In fact, technicalities to them merely delay justice," Panganiban said.
Puno: 'Two-thirds' is a fraction, not a fixed 16
Puno rejected a literal reading of the two-thirds rule. "If we give this kind of reading to Article XI, Section 3(6), the threshold of 16 senators to convict will be fixed and immutable," he said.

"However, if that is the intent, Article XI, Section 3 should have simply stated that the number of votes to convict is 16, period," Puno said. "By using two-thirds, the number of votes to convict will have to move depending on certain factors."
A strict literal reading, he warned, "may result in absurdities and may result in injustices which will defeat the purpose of the Constitution."

Puno said he follows a "contextual and functional" reading, which gives senators "the flexibility to consider circumstances that will legally prevent a senator from functioning as a member of this court."
Azcuna: 'All' means all
Azcuna was the lone dissenter in the advice given to the court.
"As long as they are members of the Senate, they constitute the denominator in computing the threshold of two-thirds, because 'all' means 'all,'" he said.

He argued that a supermajority protects officials from removal by a passing partisan majority. "Requiring two-thirds forces conviction to rest on a coalition that cuts across ordinary partisan lines, which is precisely the point," he said.

Answering a defense question, he said a count based on the full membership guards against a ruling faction jailing or charging senators to secure a conviction. "It can still be manipulated but it's not as easy," he said.
Question 2: Does the 1949 Avelino ruling apply?
Avelino v. Cuenco arose from a 1949 fight over the Senate presidency. With one senator hospitalized and another in the United States, 12 senators elected Mariano Cuenco as Senate president.
Davide and Puno said the ruling can guide the court even if it does not settle the question. Azcuna said it does not apply at all.
Davide: Not directly applicable, but has 'persuasive value'
Davide wrote that the ruling "is not directly applicable in impeachment cases. However, by analogy, it may only provide some guiding light."
He pointed out that the case dealt only with a quorum "in a Senate exclusively acting as a legislative body and performing exclusively legislative functions, and not as an impeachment court."
Still, "the Impeachment Court can consider this as having persuasive value," Davide wrote.
Puno: Not 'a perfect precedent,' but 'one of the tests'

"Strictly speaking, Your Honors, the Avelino case cannot be cited as a perfect precedent that will resolve the problem of how to properly interpret Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution," Puno said.

He gave four reasons: it settled a quorum issue and not an impeachment vote issue, it referred to the 1935 Constitution, it dealt only with a senator outside the Senate's power to compel attendance, and its core reasoning "is not as solid, not as clear, as it has to be deduced from the different opinions of the participating justices."
"Be that as it may ... its treatment of a member beyond the coercive jurisdiction of the Senate can be used as one of the tests," Puno said.
Azcuna: 'It's not applicable'
Azcuna rejected the ruling outright as it was decided based on the 1935 Constitution and involved a quorum rule that required only a majority of the Senate.
"It didn't say all the members, just majority of the Senate. And so it's not applicable," Azcuna said.
Question 3: Can senator-judges who missed the trial still vote?
The amici were most divided on this question. Davide and Panganiban said senator-judges who stay away from the trial should not be counted in the final vote.
Puno and Azcuna said senators could rely on the record, meaning transcripts and recordings of witness presentations, as well as documents submitted, to make their decision.
Davide: Never attending means never participating
A senator-judge who never attended the trial "must be deemed to have never participated in the performance of duties as such," Davide wrote.
For those who attended only partly, Davide "leaves this matter to the conscience and sense of duty of those involved."
He added that "failure to ask questions of the witness is not proof of non-participation," but "judges are to be present at all times and to listen to and reflect on the testimony of witnesses."
Panganiban: 'They should not dare vote'

Panganiban argued that the impeachment court works like a trial court, so senators must see witnesses for themselves. "The Supreme Court is a review court; it's not a trial court. But this court, the Senate acting as an impeachment court, is a trial court because you want to know the truth first — not from records, but from your experience," he said.
"If they are not in a position to know the truth, then they should not dare vote and participate because that will be unfairness to our people," Panganiban said.

Asked by Sen. Risa Hontiveros about senator-judges who willfully stay away, he said: "If you cannot, then you shouldn't be counted because you will be diminishing the effort and the voice of those who are here present, trying to find the truth and trying to be fair."
Puno: Seeing witnesses is 'ideal,' not required
Puno called the question "just a subset of the requirements of fair and impartial judges and independent tribunal."
"To determine the facts of a case, a judge need not personally see the demeanor of a witness, although that is ideal," he said.
Appellate and Supreme Court justices, he noted, "just review the testimonies of witnesses reflected in the records of the case."
Puno also suggested detained senators could follow the trial from detention. "They can see the witnesses testifying, they can be provided with the transcripts," he said.
Azcuna: 'In case of doubt, I would allow such a person to vote'
Azcuna called the matter "an internal matter that should be decided by the Senate according to its own wisdom." Absent a Senate rule, he would lean toward allowing such a vote.
"In case of doubt, I would allow such a person to vote, because this tribunal is a tribunal of record," Azcuna said.

"If he or she feels that he or she can render impartial judgment honestly according to the Constitution and the laws, then even if he missed one or two, or maybe even substantially most of the hearings, but still based on the record he or she feels that he can honestly judge the respondent, I would allow," he said.
Reminder for the impeachment court: It can interpret the Constitution
Puno reminded the court that it does not need to leave the meaning of the two-thirds rule to the Supreme Court.
He was responding to some senator-judges who had questioned whether the court could interpret the provision at all.

"My respectful submission is that the Senate as an impeachment court possesses the power to interpret the meaning and nuances of that sentence," Puno said, citing the Constitution's grant to the Senate of the "sole power to try and decide" impeachment cases.

"The decisions of the Senate impeachment court on these matters are what we call political questions — questions that are addressed to the wisdom of the senator-judge, questions that are policy matters which the senator-judges alone should decide," he said.
Responding to a question by Sen. Ping Lacson, on whether the impeachment court can avoid being accused of grave abuse of discretion by the High Court, Panganiban answered court has been "prudent."
"Your questions are very piercing, intelligent, enlightening, edifying, and we are here to give you our honest opinion on what courses of action are open to you," he said.
"As I said, you are the Supreme Court of impeachment. Your will shall prevail," he said.

articles.title: Impeachment court has sole power to decide conviction threshold -- ex-chief justices
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has the sole authority to determine the voting threshold needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte, former Supreme Court Chief Justices Reynato Puno and Artemio…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 5:29pm

The Senate impeachment court has the sole authority to determine the voting threshold needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte, former Supreme Court Chief Justices Reynato Puno and Artemio Panganiban said Wednesday.

The retired magistrates made the statements as amici curiae (friends of the court) in response to a question from Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo on whether the Senate impeachment court could legally determine the voting threshold for conviction during Day 26 of Duterte's impeachment trial.
Puno said the Senate impeachment court operates independently of the Supreme Court and derives its authority directly from the Constitution.

“That is why I explained the Senate impeachment court is not under the Supreme Court. If the Constitution wanted the Supreme Court to decide on impeachment cases, then the Senate impeachment court should have been listed under Article VIII of the Constitution on the Judiciary, not Article XI, which is Accountability of Public Officers,” Puno said.

“What does that mean? The impeachment court is given the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment, so from stage one to the last stage. That is the power given to the Senate impeachment court,” he added.

The issue over the voting threshold was raised because at least four of the 24 senators have not been participating in the impeachment proceedings, prompting questions on whether it would be fair to use all 24 senators as the denominator in determining the two-thirds threshold for conviction.
Panganiban agreed that the Constitution explicitly gives the Senate the sole power to decide impeachment cases.
“You (the Senate impeachment court) are an independent, free court. The Constitution said the Senate shall be the sole judge to try and decide impeachment cases.
"What the Constitution requires is for you, as elected representatives of the people, to make the decision. Not the Supreme Court,” Panganiban said.
He said the Constitution clearly vests the Senate, sitting as an impeachment court, with the authority to decide impeachment cases.

“If our Constitution wanted the Supreme Court to decide on impeachment cases, then it should not have designated you as the Senate impeachment court. The Constitution says that the Senate shall make the decision on impeachment cases,” Panganiban added.

At the start of the proceedings on July 6, the Senate impeachment court's presiding officer, Senate President Francis Escudero, ruled that the voting threshold for conviction should be 16 votes, or two-thirds of the Senate's 24 members.
Asked by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian whether Escudero's ruling was already set in stone, Panganiban said it was an initial ruling that could still be changed.
“The presiding officer can change his earlier position after hearing us. If he changes his opinion after being convinced, there would be no need for a vote,” Panganiban said.
Gatchalian then jokingly asked what would happen if Escudero remained “stubborn” in his position.
Puno said Escudero's ruling was only temporary and could still be changed.

“That ruling is what we call a temporary ruling. The presiding officer can change his mind and change his ruling. In the same manner, you can now vote and later on you might change your mind. It is different from a final decision of conviction or acquittal. That is final. But everything else would be tentative,” Puno said.
Escudero responded that the issue was not about being stubborn but about being circumspect.

“This is not about being stubborn. As Chief Justice Panganiban said, math is exact in the abstract but not in reality. If I change my position, someone will still appeal it and we will still have to vote on it in the end,” Escudero said.
He said a vote on the threshold would therefore be unavoidable.
“So we cannot avoid a vote, whatever my decision on this matter. That is what will happen in reality,” Escudero added. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: German drama 'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack
articles.summary: A decade after the terrorist attack on a Berlin Christmas market, a new miniseries looks into the institutional failures that allowed the deadly truck rampage to happen.

image.caption: The German miniseries 'Blindspot Berlin' premiered at the Toronto Film FestivalImage: Hubert Mican Jagd/NEUESUPER

blocks.text: A decade after the deadliest jihadist attack in Germany's history, a new six-part TV series looks at the institutional failures that allowed it to happen.

"Blindspot Berlin," which had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, follows the year-long police investigation that failed to stop Anis Amri — a Tunisian whose asylum applications had been rejected, and who was already known to German security services — from driving a hijacked truck into a crowded Christmas market at Berlin's Breitscheidplatz on December 19, 2016.

Twelve people died, including Lukasz Urban, the Polish driver Amri shot before seizing his vehicle. Dozens more were injured; a 13th victim died of their injuries in 2021. Amri fled the scene and made his way across Europe before being shot dead four days later by Italian police, near Milan, during a routine identity check.

"What happened behind the scenes of that attack is in many ways just as disturbing," says "Blindspot Berlin" director David Nawrath . "[It's] a picture of overwhelmed institutions, systemic failure and a staggering blindness to the threat that was developing right in front of our eyes."

blocks.caption: Along with the people who were killed, at least 56 more were injured in the truck attack Image: picture-alliance/dpa/M. Kappeler

blocks.text: Inside the Salafist network

Set in the year before the attack, the series follows police investigator Frank Laudin (Albrecht Schuch, of "System Crasher" and "All Quiet on the Western Front") and Isra Al-Husseini (Bayan Layla), a young officer and Arabic-language translator, as they try to infiltrate the Salafist network around Abu Walaa, the Iraqi preacher based in Hildesheim who recruited for extremist group "Islamic State" (IS). Frank recruits Murat (Tamer Trasoglu), who risks his life as an undercover informant. Inside the network, they find Amri: volatile, and getting more dangerous.

But despite repeated warnings, their bosses refuse to take the threat seriously. They dismiss Amri as a possible terrorist, in part because he is also a drug dealer, something the authorities see as incompatible with being a radical Islamist.
Fiction built on the parliamentary record

The series writers and production team closely based "Blindspot Berlin" on the facts of the Amri case, and the years-long parliamentary investigation into the institutional failures that made the attack possible. The main characters in the series — Frank, Isra and Murat — are fictionalized, but the events play out as they did in real life.

"We tried to keep as close as possible to what is known about the attack and what led to it," producer Simon Amberger told DW. "There is still a lot that isn't known, that is speculation. There we tried to leave things open."
Germany's Christmas markets open amid security concerns
Understaffed, uncoordinated, unheeded
The facts of the case are damning enough.

The parliamentary inquiry committee found that the criminal division investigating Amri and other suspects was grossly understaffed, that judicial and security agencies failed to coordinate the exchange of information, and that officials made serious errors of judgment. Amri's asylum claims were rejected, but he was never deported.

At one point the bureaucracy tipped into farce. Amri tried to leave Germany to rejoin his family and was stopped at the border, where police confiscated his passport on the grounds that he lacked the correct papers to go.
Not only a German story
The producers knew from the start that the story reached beyond Germany.

The Breitscheidplatz attack came at the end of a run of assaults across Europe: the Bataclan and coordinated shootings in Paris in 2015, the suicide bombings at Brussels airport and Maelbeek metro station, and a similar truck attack in Nice, in 2016.

blocks.caption: To prevent similar ramming attacks, security barriers are now installed around Germany's Christmas marketsImage: Jochen Tack/picture alliance

blocks.text: Despite the lessons learned in the past decade, threat levels remain high. On July 25, a man drove a van into the crowds of Christopher Street Day gay pride celebrations in Berlin, killing one and injuring dozens.

The Breitscheidplatz attack also continues to resonate today, as it raises questions on "how far a free democratic society is willing to go, how much of its freedom it is willing to sacrifice for security," says Amberger.
Fears of political misuse

He's aware, however, that a story of Islamic extremism, and the failure of the German state to protect its citizens, lands differently now, in the wake of recent elections that have seen a surge of support for the anti-immigrant, Islamophobic far-right AfD party.

"There is a danger that this story, this series, could be misused to support a simplistic, populist political agenda," Amberger admits. "But it isn't that simple. [In the series] we show how extremism arises in marginalized groups that feel isolated, unseen and powerless. The solution isn't 'stop immigration.'"
"Blindspot Berlin" premieres in Germany on public broadcaster ARD in October; its international distribution is also being planned.

articles.title: EU is set to propose ban on social media and AI chatbots for under-15s
articles.summary: The EU proposal is part of an EU Kids Act that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen will present on September 17

blocks.text: URSULA VON DER LEYEN. Lead candidate for the European conservatives in the EU election Ursula von der Leyen reacts to the announcement of the first provisional results for the European Parliament elections, at the European Parliament building, in Brussels, Belgium, June 9, 2024.
Piroschka van de Wouw/Reuters
The EU proposal is part of an EU Kids Act that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen will present on September 17

items: The European Union is set to propose a ban on social media and online platforms for children under 15 as part of the EU Kids Act to protect minors from online dangers.
The proposal includes age-appropriate access to services, with strict parental controls for children aged 3 to 14, while those 15 and older can create their own accounts.
Companies will be required to pay a supervisory fee, verify children's ages, and implement measures to avoid harmful content and addictive designs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BRUSSELS, Belgium – The European Union will propose a ban restricting under 15s from social media, video sharing platforms, AI chatbots, and online games, in the most sweeping plan yet to protect children from online dangers, a European Commission document seen by Reuters shows.
Concerns have mounted globally about the impact on children’s health and safety of major outlets, including Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, TikTok, Google’s, YouTube and ChatGPT.

The EU proposal is part of an EU Kids Act that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen will present on Thursday, September 17. The former may announce some details in her State of the Union address on upcoming EU policy on Wednesday.

“The Union’s approach should allow minors to benefit from the huge potential of digital services, while protecting them from abuse and exploitation. It needs to limit the access of tech companies to our children, and not the other way around,” the document said.

The Commission’s proposal, which will also cover video gaming platforms, allows for gradual access to the various services according to age, while the obligations imposed on the companies will depend on the type of service and the age of the children.
The Commission declined to comment.
According to the document, companies will have to pay a supervisory fee to fund regulators’ enforcement and supervision.

Children from 15 onwards can set up their own accounts under the proposal, while children between 13 and 14 can ask parents to open introductory accounts for social media and video-sharing platforms under parental control and with limited contacts and strict time limits.

Accounts for children between 3 and 12 will be fully controlled by parents and will only be for child-friendly services with strict safety standards, the document said. Under-3s would have no access to the services.
Details may still change ahead of the announcement.
The Commission will need to work out the draft with EU countries and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law.
The draft seen by Reuters sets out requirements for companies, including avoiding addictive designs and harmful feeds.
They would also have to provide tools to enable children to easily report harmful content and effective parental control tools.

Social media and video-sharing platforms will be required to verify children’s age when a user opens a new account while online games platforms will have to verify children’s age before they can download games.
The companies say they take precautions and many set a minimum age of at least 13 to sign up to social media platforms. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Palace appeals for non-violence ahead of September 21 rallies
articles.summary: Malacañang on Wednesday said that while it respected the rights of people to express their sentiments on the anticipated September 21 rallies, protestors were to refrain from breaking out in violence.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 5:21pm

Malacañang on Wednesday said that while it respected the rights of people to express their sentiments on the anticipated September 21 rallies, protestors were to refrain from breaking out in violence.
The September 21 rallies in 2025 resulted in over 100 arrests, with 93 police personnel being injured.

“Hindi naman po pinipigilan ng Pangulo at hindi hinahadlangan ang saloobin or pagsasabi ng saloobin ng ating mga kababayan sa mga ganitong klaseng pagtitipon. Pero hindi po naman kinakailangan na magkaroon ng karahasan, pananakit o pagkasawi pa ng ating mga kababayan dahil ang ating Pangulo po ay nakikinig sa bawat hinaing ng ating mga kababayan,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said.

(The President will not stop and is not blocking the sentiment or the expression of our countrymen through these types of gatherings. But there is no need for there to be violence, harm or death among our citizens because the President is listening to the concern of every citizen.)
Castro said that the Philippine National Police are ready for the upcoming rallies.
Addressing calls for President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to resign amid the multi-billion flood control scam, Castro said that the government was acting to exact accountability over the corruption scheme.
“Kumilos naman po ang Ombudsman ayon sa kanilang nakitang ebidensiya, ano pa po ba ang nais ng mga taong ito? Wala na po yata itong satisfaction,” Castro said.
(The Ombudsman acted according to the evidence they saw, what else do these people want? There seems to be no satisfaction.)

Various groups are expected to take on to the streets on September 21, which is the anniversary of the Martial Law declaration of the late dictator Ferdinand Marcos Sr. — the father and namesake of the current president.

Martial Law saw the deaths of upwards of 3,200 people, with around 70,000 more being arrested, according to Amnesty International. September 21 has since become an annual protest in the Philippines. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte personally attends ICC hearing for the first time
articles.summary: Unlike in the first two status conferences, Duterte did not waive his appearance during the 3rd conference on September 16

blocks.text: ATTENDANCE. Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court, as the court hears arguments regarding Duterte's health and ability to stand trial, while he faces murder charges related to his war on drugs, in The Hague, Netherlands, September 16 2026.
REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw/Pool
Unlike in the first two status conferences, Duterte did not waive his appearance during the 3rd conference on September 16

MANILA, Philippines – Former president Rodrigo Duterte, who’s facing three counts of crimes against humanity over his drug war, personally appeared during the third status conference hearing of his case at the International Criminal Court (ICC).
This is Duterte’s first in-person appearance, and his second overall after his online attendance during the ICC’s initial hearing on March 14, 2025.

blocks.caption: Rodrigo Duterte personally attends ICC hearing for the first time

blocks.text: Presiding Judge Joanna Korner mentioned Duterte’s attendance during the Wednesday hearing on September 16. ICC spokesperson Oriane Maillet confirmed this as well to Rappler.
As of writing, the ICC has yet to release photos or videos of Duterte during the hearing.
Unlike in the first two status conferences, Duterte did not waive his appearance this time.

“To date, no waiver request has been made by the Defence publicly. The Chamber noted in the previous Status Conference that the accused would be expected to attend the Status Conference in September,” Maillet told Rappler.
“And for that, certainly, Mr. [Peter] Haynes, we would expect Mr. Duterte to be here unless there’s some medical issue,” Korner said on June 23.
Duterte has been detained in The Hague, Netherlands since 2025, and became the first former Philippine head of state to be arrested through an order by an international tribunal.

His case is currently at the trial stage after the pre-trial chamber, on April 23, confirmed all the three charges against the former president. A day before the pre-trial chamber’s decision on the confirmation of charges, the ICC Appeals Chamber also denied with finality Duterte’s jurisdiction appeal. This cleared the way for the trial.
Duterte’s full-blown trial will begin on November 30. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with ants
articles.summary:
Prosecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menu

A South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most…

blocks.text: A South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most celebrated restaurants and its chief executive for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law.
The operator of Evett, a two-Michelin-star restaurant in the affluent Gangnam district, was fined 10m won (£5,400) and its chief executive 15m won, Newsis reported.
Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the chief executive and a 20m wonfine for the company.

The judge at Seoul’s western district court, Lee Se-chang, said the offence was “by no means light”, citing the length of time the dishes had been sold for, the restaurant’s use of them to promote itself and tests that found heavy metals above permitted levels in the ants.

He said he had taken into account that the defendants admitted the offence, that the chief executive had no previous criminal record under the food safety law, that the number of ants served appeared lower than prosecutors had calculated and that the restaurant no longer used ants.
Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, he said.
Both sides have seven days to appeal. The Guardian contacted Evett for comment.

Evett was founded by the Australian chef Joseph Lidgerwood, who has appeared on the Netflix cooking competition Culinary Class Wars and is the restaurant’s public face. He was not a defendant and was not charged.

Under South Korean food safety law, the legal duties fall on the person registered as operating the business. Ginny Kim, Lidgerwood’s wife, is registered as the company’s chief executive and was named as a defendant, alongside the company that operates the restaurant.
Only 10 insect species are approved as food ingredients in South Korea, including grasshoppers, mealworms and silkworm pupae.

Businesses wishing to use an unapproved insect must obtain temporary approval from the ministry of food and drug safety, a step the restaurant did not take. Violating the law carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison or a 50m won fine.
The ministry launched its investigation after seeing mentions of the ant dishes in blog posts and social media.

Prosecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post from April 2021, and served three to five of them atop a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink, until January 2025.
They estimated the dessert was served to 12,274 customers, using 49,096 ants, for total revenue of about 120m won.
Lawyers disputed that figure in court, arguing that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered.

The restaurant also noted that only a small number of dishes on their 15-course menu included ants, and that restaurants in countries including Denmark, the UK and Australia use ants as an ingredient.
Insect-eating is neither new nor unusual in South Korea. Beondegi, steamed silkworm pupae, has been sold from street carts for decades and remains a nostalgic popular snack for children.

articles.title: Ombudsman calls for fair reporting on Marcoleta's Sandiganbayan hearings
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday called on the media to deliver more responsible reporting after news reports allegedly created a misleading impression on the evidence presented in Senator…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 5:04pm

The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday called on the media to deliver more responsible reporting after news reports allegedly created a misleading impression on the evidence presented in Senator Rodante Marcoleta's plunder case.

The Ombudsman cited a media report that referenced a testimony from Ombudsman Luzon Field Investigation Bureau Director Maria Melinda Mananghaya-Henson, who said there was no episode that the three businessmen accused of giving Marcoleta P75 million had met with one another.

"Part of the testimony cited in the article pertains only to specific questions on whether there was evidence that the three alleged donors had personally met or communicated with one another. Let us be very clear, there is very strong evidence on record which warranted the filing of the case," the Office of the Ombudsman said.
"The ongoing hearings should be allowed to proceed without isolated portions of testimony being portrayed as determinative of the entire case," it added.
The Ombudsman said court proceedings must be understood in their entirety and parts of it cannot just be taken and turned into a different narrative.
It showed an original link to the newspaper article in question, the title of which now appears to be updated. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Iranian security forces coordinated killing, torture and sexual abuse of protesters, says Amnesty
articles.summary:
Leaked documents and testimony reveal extent of regime’s crackdown in 2022 and how it paved the way for more brutal killings of protesters this year

Iranian security forces “coordinated” the…

blocks.text: Iranian security forces “coordinated” the killing, torture and sexual abuse of hundreds of people who took part in the women-led nationwide protests in September 2022, according to leaked state documents and interviews.

Tens of thousands of people, including children, took to the streets of towns and cities across Iran after the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, after her arrest by the “morality” police for allegedly not complying with the country’s hijab regulations.

In response, the Iranian state instigated a brutal crackdown. Official statements and leaked documents cited by Amnesty reveal instructions for a “firm and severe” response. One leaked order instructed forces to “respond mercilessly and go as far as causing death”.

The rights group has now investigated and verified the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, including 56 children. It also documented the cases of 16 people who were reportedly subjected to rape while arbitrarily detained in connection with the uprising, who included six women, seven men, a 14-year-old girl and two boys aged 16 and 17.

The Amnesty report said: “State agents penetrated women and girls vaginally, anally and orally, while men and boys were penetrated anally. Victims were penetrated with wooden and metal batons, glass bottles, hosepipes and/or the sexual organs and fingers of agents.”

The harrowing findings echo testimonies gathered by the Guardian during and after the crackdown. In a Guardian report from December 2022 medics said security forces were shooting female protesters in the faces, breasts and genitals, and warned that the severity of the injuries could leave hundreds of young Iranians with permanent damage.

blocks.caption: An X-ray of a woman shot in the crotch during Iran protests in 2022, with about 200 metal balls embedded in her upper thigh and pelvic area.  Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: In testimony published in 2023, a 25-year-old protester told the Guardian she had been blindfolded and sexually assaulted during interrogation by security agents. Similar testimonies involving sexual assault and torture were reported by people interviewed following the anti-regime protests that took place in January 2026.

Amnesty’s report says years of impunity for the violent crackdown paved the way for the even more brutal crackdown on the nationwide anti-government protests in January 2026, which culminated in the deaths of thousands of protesters over 48 hours on 8 and 9 January.

Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general, said: “This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns. The agents on the streets operated within a hierarchical and coordinated chain of command linking them to officials who directed, enabled, facilitated and supported crimes committed on a massive scale.”
after newsletter promotion

Amnesty identified 87 Iranian officials, including the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, and Mohammad Bagheri, the former chief of the general staff of the armed forces, killed in an airstrike in June 2025, who it said should be investigated for “crimes against humanity”.

Amnesty also named the then minister of interior, Ahmad Vahidi, who has since become the general commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and the then deputy minister of interior for police and security, Majid Mirahmadi.

articles.title: New report reveals prevalence of physical and sexual violence in US
articles.summary:
Study finds more than half of US adults have experienced physical violence and nearly half sexual violence

In their lifetime, more than half of US adults have experienced physical violence –…

blocks.text: In their lifetime, more than half of US adults have experienced physical violence – and nearly half have experienced sexual violence, according to a startling new national study.

The study, led by researchers from Tulane University’s Newcomb Institute and the University of California, San Diego, examined experiences of physical, sexual and intimate partner violence, along with how they intersect with behavioral health, economic hardship, neighborhood safety and substance use, among other factors.
The study found that 52% of US adults have experienced physical violence during their lifetime, including cases involving a gun or knife. The rate was the same among women and men: 52% each.

Speaking to the Guardian, Anita Raj, executive director of the Newcomb Institute and co-author of the study report, said the survey pointed to the importance of assessing violence beyond crime reports.

“That’s a fraction of people who are affected,” said Raj, whose study is titled Violence in America: Findings from the 2025 United States Violence Experiences Survey (USVEX). “We also don’t want to find out about it at that point because if we’re finding out at that point, the risk for fatality has now gone up.”
USVEX surveyed 2,720 adults across all 50 states between October and December 2025 using a nationally representative sample administered by NORC at the University of Chicago.

The study was conducted in English and Spanish, with its finding arrives months after the Trace – a non-profit newsroom dedicated to reporting on gun violence – calculated that the Trump administration had terminated, redirected or delayed more than $1bn in federal grants related to gun violence, public safety, mental health and other efforts to save lives.
In the past year, one in 20 American adults (5%) experienced physical violence – and 3% reported physical abuse that did not involve a weapon, the study found.

Women most often experienced physical violence at the hands of a spouse or romantic partner, at 61%, while men most commonly experienced violence from a stranger, at 38%. Among men, 25% reported violence by a spouse or romantic partner and 24% by a family member, according to the study.
It also found both women and men most often reported experiencing physical violence at home, at 69% and 34%, respectively. Men also reported experiencing violence in public spaces at a rate of 30%.
Physical violence was also associated with significant mental health consequences.

Among those who experienced physical violence in the past year, 48% of women and 26% of men said the experience resulted in anxiety or depression. Only a minority of those affected filed formal complaints, including 10% of women and 17% of men.
The study also found that 49% of US adults have experienced sexual violence during their lifetime, with a significantly higher prevalence among women, at 68%, than men, at 29%.

In the past year, 7% of Americans – about one in 14 – experienced sexual violence, the survey found. The rate was 9% among women and 4% among men. The study noted that sexual harassment accounted for much of this violence.

Strangers were the most commonly reported perpetrators of sexual violence in the past year, accounting for 58% of cases involving women and 66% of cases involving men. Acquaintances or community members were the next most commonly reported perpetrators, at 47% for women and 41% for men, according to the study.

The locations also differed by gender. Most women who experienced sexual violence in the past year said it occurred in public spaces, at 55%, while 64% of men said it occurred at home, the study said.

Additionally, 42% of women who faced sexual violence in the past year reported suffering from depression or anxiety, while 39% of men said the violence they experienced resulted in anxiety or depression. The study also found that 4% of women and 10% of men who experienced sexual violence during the past year considered suicide.

Intimate partner violence (IPV) was also widespread, with 61% of women and 45% of men reporting that they had experienced it. Nearly one in five women, or 19%, reported potentially lethal IPV, including beating, burning, strangulation or violence involving a knife or gun – compared with 3% of men.

The study found that experiences of violence rose sharply during adolescence and young adulthood, with rates increasing during adolescence and continuing to climb into young adulthood. By this stage, nearly one-third of adults reported having experienced sexual violence.

Economic hardship was also closely linked to experiences of violence. Adults who had been evicted in the previous year were seven times more likely to report recent physical violence, three times more likely to report sexual violence and nearly five times more likely to report intimate partner violence, the study noted.

Raj on Tuesday pointed to factors such as economic status as an important metric, saying: “What we really see are what we call economic shocks that increase their very acute vulnerability. So [those are] things like not having enough money to meet basic needs like food … an eviction, or having been homeless in the past year.

“At the same time, we also see the early experiences of violence. … When you’ve had those experiences early in life, you are more vulnerable to them throughout your life, and so that’s really a piece of this.

“It shouldn’t take a fatality for you to understand risk for fatality. By assessing behaviors that women have experienced that could have killed them, you have a better understanding of how much risk for fatality from domestic violence there actually is.”

Echoing Raj, Jakana Thomas, a political science professor at the University of California, San Diego, and co-author of the study, said: “These findings show that violence prevention cannot occur in isolation. It must be part of a broader strategy that also addresses economic hardship, mental health and other forms of social inequality associated with violence.”

Raj and Thomas’s study arrived three days after a woman, her daughter, her son and his girlfriend were killed in a stabbing spree at a home in Houma, Louisiana, about 60 miles south-west of the Newcombe Institute. The man whom authorities arrested in connection with the deadly attack – which also wounded a six-year-old minor – had reportedly fathered a child with one of the victims.

Those killings occurred two years after Louisiana’s department of health warned that intimate partner violence was a “significant public health concern in the state”. The state’s rate of women murdered by men has historically been significantly higher than the national average, according to the Louisiana Coalition Against Domestic Violence.
A statement from Tulane said the new study grew out of work focused on Louisiana that Raj and her colleagues had done before then seeing same many of the same patterns then emerge nationally.

articles.title: Company behind failed Surrey oilfield project sells site at massive loss
articles.summary:
New owners apply for permission to extract oil in Horse Hill despite landmark ruling from supreme court in 2024

After years of trying to dig for oil in Surrey, the company behind the…

blocks.text: After years of trying to dig for oil in Surrey, the company behind the drilling project that was turned down in a landmark supreme court ruling has sold off the site for a fraction of the money it spent on it, and rebranded as a clean energy company.
Meanwhile, the new owners, who picked up the site for £1m, are applying, once again, for permission to dig.

UK Oil and Gas (UKOG) spent more than a decade trying to develop Horse Hill oilfields, where they said they had found 100bn barrels of oil. But in 2024 the supreme court, in a decision which has since become known as the Finch Ruling, decreed that “a planning authority should have considered the indirect downstream greenhouse gas emissions of an oil and gas project as part of its environmental impact assessment” and overturned a council decision to let expansion go ahead.

The Guardian understands that the implied value of the Horse Hill licence area reached a peak of £46m in September 2018 after UKOG agreed to buy a 14.3% economic stake from a group of vendors for £6.6m. The surging valuations given to the fields was driven by industry estimates that there could be about 9.24bn barrels of oil in the tight Jurassic shale and conventional reservoir sections within the Horse Hill licences.

Public records appear to show UKOG invested more than £25m into the site. Prior to the £1m sale, UKOG’s financial accounts showed that it had written down the value of its Horse Hill interests to just £55,360 on its balance sheet.
UKOG has now changed its name to UK Energy Group, seeking to shift its focus towards salt-cavern energy storage and other clean energy projects.

Stephen Sanderson, the company’s chief executive, said while the company still sees “potentially material resources” at Horse Hill, the divestment presented “timely and attractive opportunity to complete UKOG’s exit from the UK onshore oil and gas sector”.
The company reportedly raised £1m in 2025 to develop hydrogen-storage projects in south Dorset and Yorkshire, and a further £500,000 to acquire land for a proposed East Yorkshire salt-cavern site.

Guy Prince, the head of energy supply at energy transition thinktank Carbon Tracker, said Horse Hill was an example of “regulatory stranding”, in which climate litigation and regulatory shifts undermine the value of a fossil fuel asset.

“The same transition risk can have really radical financial consequences depending on who owns the asset,” he said. “For a major [company], it might impair one investment opportunity. But for a small company concentrated on one project like this, it just transformed the entire business.”

New owner Energy B is taking over UKOG’s application to drill for oil in Surrey. Horse Hill Developments Ltd, which it now controls, submitted a renewed planning application to Surrey county council in May for four production wells, a new oil processing area, tanker-loading facilities and a fluid reinjection well.
The proposal would allow nearly 700,000 tonnes of oil to be extracted over 20 years.
Sarah Finch, the campaigner who brought the successful legal challenge to the supreme court in 2024, said there were “serious shortcomings” with the application’s new environmental assessment.

blocks.caption: Sarah Finch, left, took her fight against Horse Hill all the way to the supreme court in 2024. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images

blocks.text: “New guidance from the government and pre-existing guidance all say that they have to place the emissions from a new proposed project within a cumulative context of all current and approved fossil fuel projects,” Finch said. “They didn’t make any attempt to do that, although the data is readily available out there.”

The application estimates that the development would result in about 2.3m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions over its lifetime, including emissions from the eventual burning of the oil, but concluded the impact was “insignificant”.
Planning documents said: “Horse Hill would account for around 0.05% of the projected UK carbon budget; an insignificant contribution that would give rise to insignificant climate change effects.”
after newsletter promotion

Finch said the developer’s argument was “false”. “Any greenhouse gas emissions are significant,” she added. “The International Energy Agency has said we can’t afford any new oil or gas. Any additional fossil fuels are going to make it impossible to stay within the 1.5C target, so [the emissions] are significant.”

The application argued that extracting up to 678,693 tonnes of oil at Horse Hill would improve energy security by reducing the UK’s reliance on imports. An Energy B spokesperson said: “At a time of global uncertainty and energy price shocks, domestic oil and gas production increases energy security.

“We are confident of meeting all the necessary legal and environmental requirements for the site. With the oil being refined in the UK and the gas serving the domestic market, the field will contribute positively to the UK economy.”
Finch disputed that argument, saying domestically produced oil was typically traded on an international market rather than necessarily supplying British consumers.
Finch said Surrey county council’s decision would be a “significant test case” for whether the climate risks of fossil fuel projects are being properly assessed after the supreme court ruling.
The local authority’s formal consultation closed on 13 July, although the council has said it will consider submissions received before it makes its decision, which could be reached this month.

Finch said the Weald Action Group would not rule out seeking another judicial review if the council approved the development. “We’re fairly confident that the environmental statement that’s been submitted isn’t compliant with the law and the new guidance,” she said.
UK Energy Group/UK Oil and Gas declined to comment.

articles.title: Amnesty report says Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in bloody 2022 protest crackdown
articles.summary: Four years after the death of a young woman whose name became synonymous with the fight for women's rights and freedom in Iran, Amnesty International says the resulting government crackdown was a…

image.caption: Iranians protest the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in 2022. In a new report Wednesday, Amnesty International said authorities committed crimes against humanity in the regime's deadly crackdown on nationwide protests. (The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Four years after the death of a young woman whose name became synonymous with the fight for women's rights and freedom in Iran, Amnesty International says the resulting government crackdown was a systemic campaign whose perpetrators continue to evade accountability.
Mahsa Amini was 22 when she died on Sept. 16, 2022, after being arrested by Iran's morality police for "unsuitable attire."

Wednesday's Amnesty report — a mammoth undertaking drawing on 270 interviews, more than 2,000 videos and extensive documentary evidence — says those same officials continue to lead violent crackdowns now. It identifies dozens of officials allegedly responsible for committing what it describes as crimes against humanity.
Its authors are demanding international action to avoid repeating the same pattern of deadly crackdowns they say has been allowed to continue for years.

"Continued global inaction on international justice sends a very dangerous message to the Iranian authorities. It effectively signals that they can continue to commit crimes against humanity with absolute impunity," Raha Bahreini, Amnesty International's Iran researcher in London, told CBC News.
"This normalization of mass protest killings in Iran must end."
Thousands killed in protests earlier this year

The U.K.-based non-governmental organization lays out the evidence it says constitutes crimes against humanity, including murder, torture, enforced disappearance, imprisonment, rape and persecution on political, gender, ethnic and religious grounds in order to crush the uprising.

While the protests earlier this year were initially triggered by economic grievances over soaring inflation and worsening living conditions rather than the death and rights abuses of women, Amnesty said the pushback reflected the same broader demands for political change and were met by the same security apparatus accused of brutally suppressing the 2022 uprising.
In the January case, U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency said it had verified 7,007 deaths linked to the protest crackdown.

"The cycles of protest crackdowns in Iran follow a very painful, familiar pattern. They dominate the news headlines for a while, governments issue statements of condemnation, and then attention fades away," Bahreini said.
Minority groups disproportionately targeted, report says
Amini, a Kurdish-Iranian woman, died three days after she fell into a coma in police custody.
Her Kurdish name Jina (or Zhina), which means "life" in Kurdish, is still used by Kurdish activists and rights groups — represented in the Woman, Life, Freedom movement slogan.
It was the protests sparked by Amini’s death that launched the pattern of unlawful killings that began in Kurdistan province, the Amnesty report says.
It found that Iranian authorities disproportionately targeted Kurdish and Baluchi communities, who largely practice Sunni Islam in a predominantly Shia nation, with "lethal repression."

Both groups reportedly suffered a "devastating share" of deaths in 2022, making up roughly 62 per cent of the total number of known victims despite representing at most 15 per cent of the country's population.
Mahsa Amini's death 'triggered 43 years of pent-up anger': Christiane Amanpour
The findings also come amid armed hostilities, since the U.S. and Israel declared war on Iran at the end of February, with talks currently stalling to end the months-long regional conflict.

While U.S. and Israeli officials have largely justified military action against Iran on security grounds — including its nuclear and missile programs — Amnesty cautioned against using the Iranian government's human rights abuses to legitimize unlawful military attacks.
In July, Trump condemned Iran's leadership after the execution of two protesters, calling officials "savages."

"Amnesty International unequivocally opposes violations of international law by all parties and rejects any attempt to instrumentalize the suffering of victims of human rights violations in Iran to justify unlawful attacks that inflict further civilian harm," said Secretary General Agnès Callamard.

items: Mahsa Amini, who died in Iranian police custody, awarded Sakharov human rights prize
What's happening in Iran? Breaking down the deadly protests shaking the country

blocks.text: Amnesty said the 2022 protests resulted in the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, which includes 56 children.

Most of the deaths recorded were people killed by security forces during protest dispersals between September and December, Amnesty said, while others died in custody, after release from custody — as in Amini’s case — or in "suspicious circumstances suggesting state responsibility."

"Consistent with long-standing patterns of denial and cover-up, the authorities have acknowledged only 202 deaths and falsely attributed most to non-state actors, 'rioters' or 'armed terrorists,' despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary," Amnesty said in a release.

The organization said it shared its findings and the list of officials identified in the report with Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and senior security officials but has not received a response.
Calls for criminal probes into 87 officials
In its report, Amnesty exposes what it describes as the chain of command behind the alleged crimes against humanity, naming a total of 87 officials it wants criminally investigated.
"The list, while not exhaustive, extends from the highest levels of Iran's security apparatus to officials operating at provincial and county level," Amnesty said in a news release.
Of the 87 individuals identified, there are 10 national-level officials and 77 officials at regional, provincial and county levels.

The report notes that among those identified is the late Supreme Leader and commander-in-chief of all armed forces, Ali Khamenei, and the late head of the Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces, Mohammad Bagheri. Both men were killed in February 2026 in air strikes carried out during the U.S.-Israeli military assault on Iran.

Amnesty International also names Ahmad Vahidi, who was interior minister at the time of the 2022 protests but became the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in March. It also listed former deputy minister of interior for police and security, Majid Mir Ahmadi.
"This investigation exposes the layers of command and co-ordination behind the Iranian authorities' deadly protest crackdowns," Callamard said.
Defiance, crackdowns in Iran a year after the protests
Spirit of resistance still alive
In spite of the deadly consequences since 2022, Bahreini said civil disobedience is now practiced much more "courageously."
Iran's hijab laws remain legally mandatory for women, but enforcement has varied in the years following the uprising.

"The Woman, Life, Freedom has had major achievements in terms of changing the society's attitude toward obeying discriminatory laws," she said, noting that authorities have concerns over another uprising if the rules are heavily enforced.
"The authorities managed to crush the street protests, but they didn't manage to eliminate the spirit of resistance and defiance."

articles.title: 3 people killed when NBC news helicopter crashes while covering Los Angeles bus accident
articles.summary: A local NBC news helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighbourhood on Tuesday and burst into flames, killing at least three people while reporters were covering the nearby crash of an SUV and a city…

image.caption: The helicopter crashed near a large storage facility in the Los Angeles neighbourhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley. (KABC-TV/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A local NBC news helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighbourhood on Tuesday and burst into flames, killing at least three people while reporters were covering the nearby crash of an SUV and a city bus, officials and the station said.
TV anchor confirms that the station's helicopter went down during live broadcast
Colleen Williams, an NBC4 Los Angeles anchor, confirmed during live broadcasts that the station's chopper went down just before 7 p.m. and two people on the helicopter were killed.
"We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it," she said, her voice shaking with emotion. Moments later their coverage abruptly cut off.

Fire officials, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and other politicians spoke during a news conference Tuesday night but gave no details on who perished in the crash. After the news conference, the mayor and other officials embraced a crying NBC reporter who also was hugged by fellow journalists.

items: TSB renews calls for updated helicopter safety rules following fatal northern Alberta crash
1 dead after plane crashes into 2 vehicles on B.C. road

blocks.text: "Losing five Angelenos is very painful," Bass said. "And I know this community of Chatsworth hit hard, will be grieving for some time."

The helicopter crashed near a large storage facility in the neighbourhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley, as news crews were covering the bus crash that left at least two people dead and six others injured, according the Los Angeles Fire Department.
At least one person killed in the helicopter crash was outside in the parking lot next to the commercial building, said Capt. Branden Silverman, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department.
Helicopter 'destroyed'
Two people were transported to a hospital, said Rico A. Gross, a fire department battalion chief. Their conditions were not immediately released.

"From the helicopter itself, it's pretty well destroyed," Silverman said. "So we are going to have to go through the rubble and see how many victims there were on board, as well as identify the helicopter; we couldn't even see a tail."
At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground burned after the helicopter caught fire, which was quickly put out, according to officials.

About two hours before the crash, an SUV slammed into the middle of a city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Photos and videos online showed half the SUV lodged into the side of an MTA bus.

NBC has confirmed the helicopter was NewsChopper4, which is operated by Angel City Air, and was used by NBCLA and Telemundo 52. The outlet said several TV news helicopters were reporting on the bush crash before the news chopper went down about 2.4 kilometres from the bus collision.

NBC4 and Telemundo 52 Los Angeles said in a statement they "are deeply saddened" to learn of the helicopter crash and extended "heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives."
Gov. Gavin Newsom thanked the emergency crews responding to both crashes and said in a post on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families."

The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said it will be investigating the cause of the helicopter crash and would be sending one of its investigators on Wednesday.
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the U.S. since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts.
