articles.title: EU chief Ursula von der Leyen says she wants Canada to become the bloc's 1st associate member
articles.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed opening a path for Canada to become the European Union's first associate member, a striking overture as U.S. President Donald…

image.caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said an expanded partnership between the European Union and Canada would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and ec

blocks.text: World·New

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed opening a path for Canada to become the European Union's first associate member, a striking overture as U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs drive Ottawa closer to Europe.
PM Carney due to address European Parliament on Thursday

"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during her annual State of the European Union address. Carney received a standing ovation from European lawmakers. He is due to address the European Parliament on Thursday.

Trump's tariffs and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have pushed Canada to seek closer economic and security ties with Europe. Carney has called for a "unique alliance" with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on U.S. trade.

Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would build on their existing free trade agreement, known as CETA, with a broader "Alliance for the Future" aimed at creating "a common prosperity and economic security space."

blocks.text: She cast that closer relationship as rooted not just in trade but in shared democratic values.

articles.title: Protesters gather outside the ICC on former President Duterte's third status conference
articles.summary: During the third status conference of the ICC Trial Chamber before the trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte, several groups of Filipino workers and residents in the Netherlands held a protest.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 4:46pm
During the third status conference of the ICC Trial Chamber before the trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte, several groups of Filipino workers and residents in the Netherlands held a protest.

They call on the Dutch and even the ICC to continue detaining Duterte, especially since the trial of the former President, who they say considered himself "untouchable," is an inspiration to the entire world.
Other groups, on the other hand, used the opportunity to call for the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte.
On the side of the former President's supporters, only a small number of people came to the ICC today for the status conference.
According to a supporter, they had no activities planned today, but he and a few others were able to enter the ICC to watch the hearing.

A few minutes before the scheduled status conference of the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III on the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte, there is still no word whether he will be present during the proceeding.
The ICC Registry has not yet made public any documents regarding the possible waiver of the defense, as well as the opposition to it by the prosecution and the lawyers of the drug war victims.
GMA News is currently seeking information from the ICC Public Affairs Unit regarding Duterte's attendance at the status conference, but to date, the office has not yet responded.

articles.byline: JOAHNA LEI CASILAO, GMA News, ANDY PENAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 4:42pm
Former President Rodrigo Duterte attended, for the first time this Wednesday, September 16, 2026, the International Criminal Court’s (ICC) status conference in his crimes against humanity case.
According to GMA stringer Andy Peñafuerte III, the former official was already seated when the judges arrived.
Unlike the previous two hearings, Duterte did not waive his appearance.

The Trial Chamber will tackle the prosecution’s case, including its list of witnesses, number of hours to be given to the prosecution, list of evidence, disclosure to the defense, and additional incidents.

It will also discuss the sitting schedule of the trial from November 30 until the Spring Recess in 2027. Aside from this, the Chamber will discuss the Registry’s proposal to have blocks of hearings with breaks and sitting hours in light of the experts’ recommendations.
Duterte is facing charges for crimes against humanity over alleged killings during his time as President and Davao City mayor.
He was arrested in March 2025 at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) Terminal 3.
The former official is currently detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen in The Hague, the Netherlands. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘It’s how Jean does business’: Fugitive developer left Jeremy Greenwood ‘high and dry’, Icac hears
articles.summary: Greenwood denies that invoices for almost $1m sent in a single day in September 2021 were ‘bogus accounts’ to cover up political donations

blocks.text: A Liberal factional figure has been left “high and dry” by fugitive property developer, Jean Nassif, but did not chase him for payments because “it’s how Jean does business”, New South Wales’ anti-corruption watchdog has heard.

Jeremy Greenwood returned to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) commission on Wednesday after Nassif made an explosive video appearance from his Beirut bedroom on Monday and Tuesday. Nassif declared he was “not corrupt”.

Icac is investigating an allegation that Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis shared in $2m in payments between 2020 and 2023 from Nassif, or his company Toplace, in exchange for political outcomes.

Greenwood and Perrottet have said payments were for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood. Greenwood has previously described an agreement, which he said was written on a purple-pink piece of paper, under which they would be paid $1m for each Toplace development they could get fast-tracked.

On Wednesday afternoon, Greenwood denied that invoices purportedly “in arrears” of almost $1m sent in a single day by Beckington to Toplace in September 2021, were “bogus accounts to cover up the scheme where Nassif is paying large amounts of money [in political donations]”.

“There’s no scheme,” he said. Greenwood, who told the commission he did not believe Beckington received all the money owed to it by Toplace before it began to pay JPG Advisory in 2022, was asked why he had not followed this up with Nassif.
“You’ve met him now,” said Greenwood. “It’s how Jean does business”.

Greenwood has told the inquiry he is a creditor of Toplace, which collapsed in 2023 after Nassif fled for Lebanon in late 2022 owing more than $1bn. On Wednesday, the commission heard that Christian Ellis was also a creditor and had publicly lodged that Beckington was owed $1.4m by Toplace for consultancy work between 2019 and 2021.
Greenwood, who has admitted to being in contact with Ellis during the inquiry, was asked if he had discussed with him “the proposition you were owed over $1m” by Nassif.
“I mean we’ve certainly discussed the fact that Jean, we believe, left us high and dry,” he said.

Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC put it to him that it “is not something that you would want to openly disclose, the consultancy work you did with Jean Nassif”. Greenwood said he had “no issue disclosing that I worked for Toplace”.
Questions over Anita Perrottet work

On Wednesday morning, Greenwood was asked about his previous evidence on advice he said Anita Perrottet, sister-in-law of the former premier, gave to lobbying firms Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.
Dwyer has alleged invoices of $660,999 paid to Anita Perrottet’s company, Macquarie Consulting, over two and a half years were her husband, Charles Perrottet’s, share of the money from Nassif.

Anita Perrottet has told the watchdog payments were for “strategic and marketing advice” she provided; while Charles Perrottet has said they were “holistic” payments covering his advice to Nassif on his developments as well as his wife’s work.

Greenwood has previously told the commission Anita’s advice, for which the commission has no written evidence, provided a “mum’s perspective”. He said after first being contracted by Beckington in 2020, she may have come up with the term “zero unnecessary euthanasia” for greyhounds, and given advice about discouraging minors from vaping, including removing flavours such as bubble gum, as well as black market regulation.

On Wednesday, Dwyer took Greenwood to 2017 recommendations by the NSW greyhound industry reform panel, which included the phrase “zero unnecessary euthanasia”, suggesting to Greenwood he had “outsmarted [him]self by coming up with that false evidence when it’s clearly a term used in a document years earlier”.

“I disagree,” Greenwood replied. Dwyer showed Greenwood a submission by Philip Morris to a 2020 senate inquiry which referenced measures to regulate the illicit tobacco trade and a 2019 report committing to applying guidelines to prevent youth access to vapes.
Greenwood said he had read the submission by Philip Morris, a client of his, but rejected Dwyer’s suggestion it “makes a mockery” of his evidence about Anita Perrottet’s advice.
After Dwyer asked him how old Anita Perrottet’s children were at the time she provided advice on vaping, Greenwood said he did not know, and did not think it was relevant.
after newsletter promotion
The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened to tell Greenwood he was “not here to debate with counsel assisting” but to “answer the question”. Greenwood said: “I presume they’re under 10.”
Dwyer, telling Greenwood that Anita Perrottet’s children were around two and three at the time, asked: “Did she give you a mum’s perspective on deterring under-fives from vaping?
“No,” Greenwood replied.

Dwyer said: “Your evidence is ridiculous, can I suggest to you, that Anita Perrottet contributed to a debate that had been the subject of professional reports … for many years before you say you brought Anita Perrottet on board.” Greenwood disagreed.
Gleeson made a non-publication order over a racist message Greenwood had sent in 2020 about the chief of staff of then-treasurer Dominic Perrottet.

Ellis had shared a screenshot of messages with Greenwood in which he had written to ask to be connected with a treasury staff member on behalf of Toplace, to which the chief of staff responded: “We have no interest in doing favours for developers. All proposals will go through proper planning processes and be assessed on its merits.”

Gleeson paused proceedings, making a direction that it was in the public interest that a “racist remark” Greenwood sent to Ellis about the chief of staff be suppressed. Greenwood accepted Dwyer’s suggestion that the comment was “highly offensive”.
Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year and is not expected to appear. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

On Wednesday afternoon, Greenwood was asked about folders shared by Anita Perrottet with him via email in March 2023 following parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe, titled “Greyhounds”, “British Tobacco” and “Catholic Cemeteries”.

Anita Perrottet previously told the commission she ceased to work for JPG Advisory before the parliamentary inquiry. After Dwyer alleged that the empty folders which were created as a “false documents trail” – which Anita Perrottet has denied – Greenwood said he could not speculate.
Dwyer later asked: “There is no reason that you can think of to send you empty folders at any time, is there?”
“No, unless you thought in future there might be a need to fill them,” said Greenwood.

Greenwood was not released from his summons at the end of his evidence on Wednesday but not is currently scheduled to appear again before the commission. As Dwyer’s questioning of Greenwood concluded on Wednesday, she put it to him that he had put Anita Perrottet “a very difficult position … because you and others, but let’s stick with you, were party to her lying to this [commission]”. Greenwood disagreed.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

articles.title: European Union opens door for Canada to become first associate member
articles.summary: Commission president says partnership will create ‘common prosperity’ based on shared democratic values

blocks.text: The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, told the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, on Wednesday that she wants to open the door for his country to become the EU’s first associate member.

The overture comes as Trump’s tariffs and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have pushed Ottawa to seek closer economic and security ties with Europe. Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.

“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen told Carney during her annual state of the European Union address. Carney received a standing ovation from European lawmakers. He is due to address the European parliament on Thursday.

Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would build on their existing free trade agreement, known as Ceta, with a broader “alliance for the future” aimed at creating “a common prosperity and economic security space”.

The commission president described that closer relationship as rooted not just in trade but in shared democratic values. “Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” von der Leyen said.
“We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us. That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.”

Von der Leyen said the expanded partnership would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defence production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. “In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca
articles.summary: The Houthis deny targeting the Islamic holy city after the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen accuses them of a "disgraceful act".

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
Turki al-Maliki said the targeting of Mecca, which is the home of Islam's most sacred shrine and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage, was a "disgraceful act".

The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression".
But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies".

"There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said.
Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.
He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province.

There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour".
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city.

Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities.
The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.

Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal.

The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.
A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."

The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.
Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.
More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
"Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Ex-SC Chief Justice Panganiban: Absent senator-judges should inhibit
articles.summary: Retired Supreme Court (SC) Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban on Wednesday said senator-judges who have been continuously absent from Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial should voluntarily…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 16, 2026 4:34pm

Retired Supreme Court (SC) Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban on Wednesday said senator-judges who have been continuously absent from Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial should voluntarily inhibit from voting.

He made the remark when he was asked, as one of four amici curiae (friends of the court), whether senator-judges who had taken their oaths but had been continuously absent from the proceedings should still be counted in determining the number of votes needed for conviction.
“So, if I were in their position, because they are not in a position to render a truthful and fair judgment, I would even voluntarily inhibit from voting,” Panganiban said.
“For me, it is a practical matter for the people. I will no longer cite cases from the SC. There are many, both for and against. But I appeal to your sense of right and wrong,” he added.

The Senate impeachment court tapped four retired Supreme Court justices as amici curiae to provide independent legal opinions on the disputed voting threshold for convicting Duterte, amid questions over whether the two-thirds threshold should be based on all 24 senators or only those participating in the impeachment trial.
Panganiban maintained that senator-judges who are not present during the proceedings cannot render a fair judgment and should therefore not be counted.
“Because you will be diminishing the effort and the voice of those who are here present, trying to find the truth and trying to be fair,” he said.
Four of the 24 senators have been unable to regularly attend the Duterte impeachment trial: Senators Jinggoy Estrada, Rodante Marcoleta, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa and Loren Legarda.

Estrada and Marcoleta are detained in connection with separate criminal cases. Estrada is facing a P573-million plunder case and a graft case, while Marcoleta is detained over a P75-million plunder case.

Dela Rosa has been absent from the Senate amid an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant related to the ICC's investigation into alleged crimes against humanity linked to former President Rodrigo Duterte's anti-drug campaign. He left the Senate premises on May 14 after authorities attempted to serve the warrant and has not appeared in public since.
Legarda, meanwhile, has been on medical leave abroad. She had been absent from the impeachment proceedings and was reported to have extended her medical leave through Sept. 2.
Marcoleta previously insisted that he retains his voting capacity as a senator-judge.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: LIVE: ICC third status conference for ex-president Rodrigo Duterte
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court is holding the third status conference in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte on Wednesday, September 16.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 4:30pm
MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court is holding the third status conference in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte on Wednesday, September 16.
Duterte is attending the hearing for the first time after waiving his appearance during the previous two status conferences.

The trial chamber is expected to discuss the prosecution's case, including its list of witnesses, the number of hours to be allotted to the prosecution, its list of evidence, disclosure to the defense and additional incidents.

The chamber will also discuss the trial schedule from November 30 until the Spring Recess in 2027, as well as the Registry's proposal to hold blocks of hearings with breaks and sitting hours based on experts' recommendations.

The case stems from the ICC's investigation into alleged crimes against humanity linked to killings during Duterte's anti-drug campaign. Prosecutors have charged him with three counts of crimes against humanity involving at least 76 alleged murders between 2013 and 2018.
Duterte was arrested in Manila in March 2025 and flown to the Netherlands, where he remains detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen.

articles.title: 'It should be exposed': Survivor calls on church to release treatment records of abusive priests
articles.summary: A man abused by a notorious Catholic priest is joining others in calling on the church to release its records related to a controversial therapy centre in Ontario, where abusive priests were sent for…

image.caption: John Doe was abused by Father George Ansell Smith for more than three years, starting when he was just six. He's been locked in a lawsuit with the church for nearly 13 years. (Ted Dillon/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

A man abused by a notorious Catholic priest is joining others in calling on the church to release its records related to a controversial therapy centre in Ontario, where abusive priests were sent for decades. His abuser was sent there in 1992, and returned to work for nearly 20 years.
Father George Ansel Smith sent for therapy in 1992, returned to work for nearly 20 years
A man who was abused by a notorious Catholic priest in Newfoundland is joining other voices calling on the church to release its records on abusive priests sent away for treatment.
The man can only be identified as John Doe. He was abused by Father George Ansel Smith as a young boy on the west coast of Newfoundland in the 1970s.

Court records show Smith was sent to the Southdown Institute — an Ontario therapy centre offering a range of services for priests dealing with issues ranging from depression and alcoholism to pedophilia — in 1992.
He returned to the priesthood for nearly 20 years, until John Doe and a dozen other men came forward with allegations starting in 2011.

"I think it should be exposed for everybody to see the truth,” John Doe told CBC News. “There are file cabinets and rooms full of this stuff in every parish and every diocese. It needs to just be exposed for what it is, and let people start living their lives and move on."

items: 'To avoid scandal': Unearthed letters show how N.L. bishop handled allegations in Baie Verte
Church should open its records on abusive priests sent away for therapy, advocate says

blocks.text: John Doe spoke to CBC News following an article published last month, which detailed letters uncovered in a new court filing in Grand Falls-Windsor. The letters show the former bishop of Grand Falls exchanging letters with the executive director of Southdown in 1970, speaking about a priest who was removed from a rural parish over concerns about his "relationships" with boys.
The letters were not unearthed during the Winter Commission in 1990, which examined a surge of clergy abuse cases. They were not part of the priest's criminal trial, either.

In the wake of the story, prominent clergy abuse advocate and survivor Gemma Hickey called on the church to turn over its records for independent examination, so the public could know once and for all which priests were sent away for treatment, what Southdown recommended, and whether or not the church adhered to those recommendations.
John Doe agrees.

“I’m not surprised," he said. "I mean there’s probably more of this stuff kicking around. How many people’s lives have to be ruined before somebody says we were wrong and we’re going to atone for that now?”
Lawsuit still not settled, nearly 13 years on
Smith was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2013. He served a fraction of that time before being released on parole.

John Doe sued the Diocese of Corner Brook and Labrador (formerly known as the Diocese of St. George's) nearly 13 years ago, alleging it knew or ought to have known that Smith was a risk to children and its negligence resulted in him being abused.

He watched with mixed feelings as the Archdiocese of St. John's was forced to sell off properties to settle abuse cases on the east coast, while the church continued fighting him on the other side of the island.

John Doe said he called the bishop of Corner Brook and Labrador two years ago, and urged him to sit down with their lawyers to find a resolution. He said the bishop believed the case had already been settled, but was confusing Smith with another abusive priest whose case forced the diocese to file for bankruptcy protection in 2005.

"I said, well, I think that you need to sit down with the lawyers and really have a good conversation with them and, you know, expose it for what it is," John Doe said. "And if you have any decency at all, that's what you'll do. No such luck."
CBC News has requested comment from the Diocese of Corner Brook and Labrador. No response has been received as of publishing time.

items: Full parole for former priest, 4 years into 11-year sentence
'Get it done': Man who sued Catholic church pleads for settlement as case nears 10 years

blocks.text: John Doe said he won't be able to really begin healing until the case is settled. Small parts of daily life — like seeing children playing — can still pull him back into the past. He still wakes up screaming and fighting in the middle of the night, dreaming of the abuse he endured as a child.
If the church wants to make amends, John Doe said turning over the files on Smith and other abusive priests would be a good place to start.
"At some point, please, please, just let us have some peace. I just want a conclusion. How long does it have to go on? How long do I have to be tortured?”

articles.title: Von der Leyen eyes Canada as EU's first 'associate member'
articles.summary: EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU and Canada saw the world with the same eyes. At her annual State of the Union address, she said the bloc was dealing with an "openly hostile world."

image.caption: Von der Leyen said she wants Canada to be an 'associate member' of the EUImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union was opening the door for ‌Canada ⁠to ⁠become its first associate member — a position that the bloc would have to create from scratch.
Von der Leyen's comments came during her annual speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, while Candanian Prime Minister Mark Carney was in attendance.
This comes days after the Wall Street Journal reported that Carney was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc, a position that does not currently exist.
Earlier this week, Carney responded to the story, saying he sought a "unique alliance"with the bloc and not a membership.

"Partnerships are a ​strategic ‌choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture ‌in the international rules-based system," ‌von ​der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union ​address.

"We see the world with the same ⁠eyes: ​from AI ​to climate change, from the Arctic ​to geopolitics. And ‌we have stood together: on Ukraine, on ​defense, ⁠on raw materials and on supply chains. ⁠But ​above all ... Europe and Canada believe in democracy," she said.
The EU and Canada, which have already grown close amid conflicts and trade wars, are looking to partner with each other to diversify from China and the United States respectively.
As Trump menaces, some think Canada should join the EU
Warning against an 'openly hostile world'
Von der Leyen called for an independent European Union amid an "openly hostile world," in her speech on Wednesday.

"'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' — this is how British author Charles Dickens described Europe in the days of the French Revolution, and it is also a fair description of the world we live in," she said, beginning her address.
"The state of our union is the strongest it has ever been. The state of our union can also feel as precarious as it has ever been," she said.

blocks.caption: Von der Leyen was first elected president of the European Commission in 2019 and then again in 2024Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Von der Leyen warned against "an openly hostile world" and "frayed relationships" while speaking of Russia's war against Ukraine and not directly mentioning the EU's increasingly strained relationship with the US.

"A territorial war ‌of aggression is ‌raging ​on our continent; others have erupted nearby. A ​fight for industrial capacities is shaping ⁠global ​competition. And ​a battle of ​narratives is seeking ‌to weaken confidence in ​Europe," ⁠von der Leyen said.
Von der Leyen announces new European corporation on critical raw material
Von der Leyen, now in her second five-year term as commission president, stressed on the need to maintain European independence in various sectors including energy and raw material.
"We still have too many dangerous dependencies" she said adding the EU was still 80% dependent on China for many critical raw materials.
"We need to urgently procure and build up reserves. No country can do this on its own so we need to think differently," she said, hinting at global partnerships without mentioning nations.

"This is why we will establish a new European corporation on critical raw material. It will help us obtain and stockpile what we need ... Not only our industry depends on this but also our independence and security," she said.
As for China, the president warned the bloc would "use all tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship".

"Our trade deficit with China is now one billion euros a day. It has reached a tipping point. Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," she said. "Words are good. But deeds are better."
Future 'depends' on how EU tackles climate change, AI
Speaking of challenges, von der Leyen said the future of the 27-nation bloc depends on how it manages climate change and artificial intelligence.

"Our future prosperity and security will greatly depend on how we manage the tipping points of our time: climate change and AI," she said, promising a new "heatwave plan" following Europe's deadly summer, and a push for the bloc to help "pace the frontier" of AI development.
Von der Leyen, a mother of seven, also proposed sweeping restrictions on children's access to social media.
Under the proposal, children under 13 would be barred from accessing such services, while those aged 13 to 15 would be allowed to use restricted "mini accounts" supervised by a parent or guardian.
"I am aware that many perceive the power of Big Tech as overwhelming and impossible to roll back. I disagree," von der Leyen said.

articles.title: How hotter weather is making us poorer
articles.summary: Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.

image.caption: We are already paying a price for burning fossil fuelsImage: Robin Utrecht/picture alliance

blocks.text: The last 11 years have been the planet's hottest on record. This changing climate is manifested in extreme weather events like heat waves and wildfires. But less obvious are the higher prices and lower wages linked to a heating world.

According to a 2026 studyby the MIT Sloan School of Management and UCLA School of Law, climate change has already driven up average American household expenses by $900 (€780) a year — rising to above $1,300 for one in ten US counties.

These costs would not exist in a world without climate change. They include escalating home insurance ($600 higher on average), increasing state and federal taxes due to disaster recovery costs, or health impacts from wildfire smoke, for example.
"Climate inaction isn't just an environmental failure; it acts like a tax on every American household," wrote the researchers .

blocks.caption: An 8-month drought in California sparked catastrophic wildfires in 2025. But heat is also burning a hole in personal wealthImage: Mike Blake/REUTERS

blocks.text: How climate change is already hitting incomes

A 2024 report by Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact estimated that climate damages to agriculture, infrastructure, health and productivity could cost the world economy US$38 trillion a year by 2050.
But how have climate-driven weather extremes already impacted salaries and household budgets?

"If we can't figure out what climate change is already costing us with the data we have, projecting the future becomes almost hopeless," said Derek Lemoine, an economics professor from the University of Arizona who has estimated a 12% reduction in US incomes as global temperatures have risen. This is also compared to a non-climate change scenario.
Lemoine shows how temperature extremes in one US county are having cascading economic impacts in distant locations with milder weather due to interconnected trade and supply chains.
"Much work studies climate change as if it changes weather in only one year and one location at a time," Lemoine told DW.

Instead, he wants to understand how, if a heat wave wipes out corn crops across America, other industries that rely on that corn, including livestock and food producers, will be impacted as the commodity becomes scarcer and increases in price.

blocks.caption: Drought-affected agriculture is having compounding economics impactsImage: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: "As your costs have gone up," said Lemoine of producers impacted across the corn supply chain, "that's going to serve to make the income of everyone who depends on you go down."

Climate's impact on trade is also being felt in Germany, where record low water levels on the Rhine River — the busiest inland trade waterway in Europe — could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter of 2026, noted the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in July.

Prolonged dry weather linked to climate change is to blame as shipping capacity drops to as low as 15% on the river that connects Europe's largest port in Rotterdam, the Netherlands with much of western Germany.
Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships
Compounding existing economic pressures
One Australian study also looks at how broad climate changes, rather than local shocks from single extreme weather events, have gradually led to a decrease in productivity and economic output.

Timothy Neal, a researcher at the Institute for Climate Risk & Response at the University of New South Wales in Australia, co-authored the reportshowing that global heating reduced economic output in the state of NSW by an average of around 18%, or the equivalent of $21,288 Australian dollars (€12,974) per person in 2024.
"The damage has already been quite severe," Neal told DW, adding that in a non-warming scenario, citizens would enjoy "lower food prices" and "lower poverty."

The report refers to droughts in parts of NSW in the mid-late 2010s that reduced productivity across the whole state by up to A$10 billion due to lower agricultural yields and farm incomes, higher water costs and increased reliance on government assistance.
These financial impacts compounded through the state economy over time, influencing the cost of food, insurance and infrastructure maintenance.
In the words of the report, these effects also "compound existing economic pressures and contribute to widening disparities between regions," meaning an increase in income and wealth inequality.

blocks.caption: Putting planet-heating CO2 in the atmosphere is compounding economic stagnationImage: Stefan Ziese/imagebroker/IMAGO

blocks.text: Can climate adaptation limit costs?

"Climate change action should not be seen as a predominantly environmental, but also economically sensible," said Frank Jotzo, an economist at the NSW Net Zero Commission, which works to decarbonize the state and commissioned the above study.

Referring to "defensive climate investments" such as reinforcing roads, railways and shipping infrastructure to adapt to a hotter world, Jotzo added that "if it wasn't for climate change, we could be putting that money and that effort into other things."
However, adaptation efforts such as the greening of cities to reduce heat island effects will be vital in order to head off much worse future economic impacts.
The 2026 European heat waves, for example, have already cost around €180 billion, which is the EU's entire projected economic growth for the year, according to one analysis.

Adaptation will also involve strengthening the hospital and medical system to counteract the health effects of heat waves that also reduce productivity as heat-stressed employees tire or struggle to sleep, Jotzo noted.

blocks.caption: Workers around the world are losing productivity due to extreme heatImage: Assad Hani/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: But Lemoine says that adaptation to climate-driven economic decline is so "costly in its own right" that it could exacerbate income loss and be ineffective if not done comprehensively.
Only when "all places" are insulated from weather extremes, can the cascading economic impacts be addressed, he says.

Nonetheless, both adaptation and a rapid reduction of planet-heating emissions are together required to avoid climate-driven income loss that will worsen if warming outstrips Paris climate agreement targets.
"Unchecked climate change would create a permanent drain on wages and productivity," said Jotzo.
The economic cost of climate change and how to adapt

MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) will hold its third status conference on former president Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes against humanity case on Wednesday, September 16.
A status conference is where parties discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial.

So far, the court has held two conferences: on May 27, when it announced that the trial will begin on November 30, and then on June 23, when the chamber cautioned lawyers against granting media interviews.
For this third conference, the chamber has the following agenda:

articles.title: Former pro-Duterte vlogger is latest Marcos official
articles.summary: The vlogger and political commentator behind 'Thinking Pinoy' is now an assistant secretary in Malacañang under Cabinet Secretary Benhur Abalos

blocks.text: PALACE. Malacañang Palace riverside facade in 2013.
Presidential Museum and Library
The vlogger and political commentator behind 'Thinking Pinoy' is now an assistant secretary in Malacañang under Cabinet Secretary Benhur Abalos

items: Rey Joseph 'RJ' Pengson Nieto, known as 'Thinking Pinoy,' was appointed assistant secretary under the Office of the Cabinet Secretary in the Marcos administration on September 1, 2023.
Nieto has faced legal issues, including a conviction for violating the Data Privacy Act related to doxxing.
His exact role in the Cabinet Secretary's office is still undefined, and he has expressed a desire to apply his academic training in mathematics and public policy to his new position.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Rey Joseph “RJ” Pengson Nieto, more popularly known for his online persona “Thinking Pinoy,” is the latest official in the Marcos administration. Nieto was appointed assistant secretary under the Office of the Cabinet Secretary.
He was appointed on September 1, but the appointment was made public and confirmed by Malacañang on Wednesday, September 16.

Nieto is best known in the public, perhaps, for being a staunch supporter of former president Rodrigo Duterte, whom the Marcos adminsitration sent to the Netherlands to face charges of crimes against humanity related to Duterte’s bloody drug war.

Although President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. was once closely allied with the Dutertes — through 2022 running mate Vice President Sara Duterte, primarily — he did not have close ties with the former president himself. The older Duterte, in fact, had claimed the younger Marcos was a drug addict and latched on to the claim even when Marcos assumed office.
In a briefing with reporters, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro sought to downplay the seeming irony of Nieto’s appointment, given his past affiliations.

“Even before sinabi po natin na ang Pangulo po ay hindi tumitingin sa kulay. Kung kayo po ay makikitang magiging asset sa gobyerno para mas maging maganda ang serbisyo ng isang ahensiya hindi po mag-aatubili ang Pangulo na kayo ay kunin provided na ang puso po ninyo kahit anong inyong kulay dapat ay sa taumbayan at sa bansa hindi sa isang tao o sa isang dati ninyong tinataguyod. So, dapat ang focus ay bansa at ang taumbayan,” said Castro.

(Even before, the President had said he pays no mind to affiliations. If a person is an asset to the government in order for an agency’s services to improve, the President does not hesitate to hire that person provided their heart, no matter their affiliation, is for the people and for the country and not for one person or advocacy. So the focus should be on the people and the country.)
Castro could not say the exact role of Nieto in the Office of the Cabinet Secretary, which is headed by former interior chief Benhur Abalos.

Abalos’ role is to bridge an apparent gap between the Palace and the populace — at a time when Marcos’ approval and trust ratings are low, and with just less than two years left in the administration.

Nieto’s appointment does not come as a total surprise. When the Marcos-Duterte alliance, Nieto as associated, too, with Malacañang and First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos. After former senator Antonio Trillanes IV sued Nieto for cyberlibel, Araneta-Marcos’ law firm had apparently taken on his case pro-bono. The latter was revealed only recently, when Marcos was in power.

In 2023, a Makati court found Nieto guilty of violating the Data Privacy Act of 2012 for doxxing Jover Laurio, who was, upon the publication of a 2017 post, running the blog Pinoy Ako Blog anonymously.

Nieto once ran the popular Thinking Pinoy page, where he would regularly go live and provide commentary on top political events. His political commentary stopped when he started pursuing an undergraduate degree at the University of Bristol in 2023. The Thinking Pinoy Youtube page appears to have been scrubbed off of previous videos.
In a post on Facebook, Nieto said his exact role under Abalos has yet to be defined formally.

“I spent the past years studying mathematics in the University of Bristol. That training taught me to look carefully at evidence, systems and complex problems. Sana magamit ko iyon sa trabaho (I hope to use that in this job). At the same time, I know that government is not a classroom. Marami pa rin akong kailangang matutunan (I have much to learn). This is also why I am doing a part-time MSc in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Public Policy at UCL, pang-alalay sa trabaho (to aid me in this job),” he said.
Abalos has yet to respond to our inquiries on the role Nieto will play in his office. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Key events

18m agoUK inflation rises to 3.1% as motor fuel prices jump by almost a quarter
32m agoLisa Nandy brands Musk’s X a ‘disgrace’ as she pledges crackdown on social media doxxing

blocks.text: Piddington, small Oxfordshire village, votes for independence in symbolic referendum in protest over migrant camp
An Oxfordshire village which could house more than 1,000 asylum seekers has voted overwhelmingly to become an independent state in a symbolic “referendum”, the Press Association reports. PA says:

double quotation markThe people of Piddington have voted to secede from the UK after the government announced plans to house 1,256 male asylum seekers at a nearby former military base. Some 285 villagers backed “independence”, with a turnout of nearly 92%. Only 26 residents voted against the motion, with one spoiled ballot recorded. The result was announced by a returning officer to an audience of dozens of journalists and residents gathered outside the village hall this morning.

blocks.caption: Returning officer Susannah Parden announcing the result of the symbolic “referendum” in the village of Piddington, Oxfordshire this morning. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA
An aerial view of Piddington. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: UK inflation rises to 3.1% as motor fuel prices jump by almost a quarter
UK inflation has returned above 3% as soaring fuel and transport prices triggered by the Iran war heap renewed pressure on British households, Richard Partington reports.
Lisa Nandy brands Musk’s X a ‘disgrace’ as she pledges crackdown on social media doxxing

Good morning. We will be hearing from Andy Burnham today because he is back at work having taken time off following the death of his father. And already we have heard from Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, who has been doing a media round.
She has condemned Elon Musk’s social media platform, X, describing it as an “absolute disgrace”.

Nandy was talking about what social media companies are doing to stop people using their platforms to post intimidatory messages online, in particular posting private information like an address that might put someone at risk (doxxing). Yesterday Nandy hosted a meeting with social media companies about this, partly prompted by the abuse RNLI volunteers have been getting online by anti-migrant vigilantes who hate the lifeboat service for the role it plays protecting people on small boats at risk of drowning.
Speaking on Times Radio this morning, Nandy said:

double quotation markI had the social media companies in to see me yesterday to talk to them about their responsibilities in this regard. All of the different social media companies have completely different terms of service, different standards that they apply to online hatred directed at individuals. Some of them will automatically remove that content. Some of them, frankly, won’t. X didn’t even bother to turn up yesterday, which I think is an absolute disgrace.
Nandy said she was determined to stop doxxing.

double quotation markI have made a commitment to the RNLI and to, not just charities but public sector workers, police officers, and others who are being routinely harassed and abused online in the course of work, that we will tighten up the law. We will make sure that where, for example, people’s addresses are being published online, that we just do not allow that to happen, that those things will have to be either blocked or taken down immediately. We cannot have a situation where not just charity volunteers, but shop workers and social workers and police officers are being routinely harassed online in the course of their work.
I will post more from her interviews shortly.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Morning: Andy Burnham is visiting a factory in the south-east of England.
Late morning: Burnham meets Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general, in Oxfordshire.
11.30am: Simon Case, the former cabinet secretary, gives evidence to the Lords constitutional committee on constitutional safeguards.
12.30pm: Alex Burghart, the Tory deputy leader, and Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, speak at Policy Exchange’s Britain and the EU: After the Reset event.
Also, during the day Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, is doing a round of interviews with regional media ahead of his party’s conference, which starts at the weekend.

articles.title: Mayors and other local leaders could be given powers to oversee water firms
articles.summary:
Move would mean some input on companies’ spending and holding bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges

Mayors and other local politicians could be given powers to oversee water…

blocks.text: Mayors and other local politicians could be given powers to oversee water companies under plans being considered by the UK government to bring utilities under greater public control.
Local leaders would have the power to direct some parts of water companies’ spending and hold bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges as part of the proposals.
It comes as Andy Burnham faces growing pressure to improve the oversight of the water industry, with millions of households facing steep bill increases, leaking infrastructure and sewage spills.
Giving local political leaders more authority over the sector was a key recommendation in Sir Jon Cunliffe’s landmark review of water companies last year.
The review found it would “represent a significant change, and ensure that local voices, customers and experts have stronger authority over companies’ boards’ decisions on investment priorities”.
These regional authorities could include a local government figure, a mayor, an independent chair, experts and other representatives to cover affected sectors such as transport and agriculture.

While there have been no firm decisions yet, officials in the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs are keen on the idea, according to the BBC. It reported that the plan was among a number of ideas that the government was exploring to introduce greater public control of water companies.

Burnham has repeatedly promised to take public utilities into public control, including water companies. Before he became MP for Makerfield, he told the Guardian that he intended to nationalise Thames Water, the water company that serves 16 million customers and has been on the verge of collapse for more than two years.

At the end of March the regulated value of Thames’s assets was estimated at £23bn, while its net debt increased to £18.5bn. Ministers are considering whether to put the company into special administration or accept a solution put forward by creditors to maintain private sector control after a debt write-off.

In the meantime, customer dissatisfaction with the water industry has continued to grow. The number of complaints made by households about water companies is up 48% year on year, according to the Consumer Council for Water, the steepest annual rise in two decades.
after newsletter promotion

Mike Keil, CCW’s chief executive, said the numbers reflect “just how dissatisfied many people still are with the state of the water sector and the enormous task water companies face in rebuilding consumer trust”.

A government spokesperson said: “Our water industry has not been working for people for far too long. We’re bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment.”

articles.title: Is Donald 'drill, baby, drill' Trump helping the world transition away from oil?

image.caption: Donald Trump, shown here speaking in Pennsylvania on Oct. 14, 2024, was very pro-oil on the U.S. presidential election campaign trail. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: While running for the U.S. presidency in 2024, Donald Trump promised to do almost anything to benefit the oil industry. His slogan: "Drill, baby, drill."

But his bold actions since retaking office have in many ways had the opposite effect. While oil companies rake in windfall revenues, Trump's punitive tariffs on China and the price shocks from the war he started with Iran in February have driven many countries to consider the upsides of renewable energy.

"This is Economics 101. If you increase the price of a good and make it riskier, then you will drive people to search for alternatives," said Kingsmill Bond, director of global energy think-tank Ember. "That's exactly what's been happening."

One of the most obvious examples is electric vehicles. A report released last month by the International Energy Agency (IEA) found the global EV market rebounded in the second quarter of this year, even as overall car sales declined.

Statistics collected by Ember show that EV exports from China, the world's biggest EV producer, between March-May 2025 and March-May 2026 spiked — up 117 per cent in Brazil, 127 per cent in South Korea, 175 per cent in Australia and 220 per cent in Italy.

Countries are also adapting their energy grids to the new reality. Earlier this year, the U.K.'s largest energy supplier reported a 50 per cent increase in solar panel sales, year over year, while rising energy costs in Asia have boosted rooftop solar. Even as Canada looks to expand investment in pipelines, the government has announced a nuclear strategy aimed at doubling the electrical grid's capacity by 2050.
"EVs and batteries and solar panels are flying out the door, because people want an alternative," Bond said.
Countries seeking energy security

As Bond points out, the broader energy transition has been underway for a while. In its review of 2025, for example, Ember noted that renewables produced more than one-third of global electricity generation, "overtaking coal power for the first time in 100 years."
But the Iran war gave people the world over new incentive to consider clean energy.

Iran's response to the U.S.-Israeli attacks that began in February was to block the transit of one-fifth of the world's oil through the Strait of Hormuz. As the price of oil rose to nearly $120 US a barrel, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it "the second fossil fuel crisis in just a few years," after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"There is one thing that all these events are making clear," she said. "We are paying a very high price for our overdependency on fossil fuels."
Saudi Arabia shuts key oil pipeline after drone attack launched from inside Iraq
This seems to be a lesson many countries have learned — particularly in Asia.

For example, Thailand has turned to solar in lieu of rising natural gas prices. Soon after the Iran war began, the Philippines declared an energy emergency and its government signed executive orders to speed up grid connections and a number of projects aimed at creating 1.4 gigawatts of renewable energy (roughly enough to power one million homes).

From an environmental perspective, the responses to the Iran war's energy shocks haven't all been positive; coal usage is projected to hit a record high this year, according to the IEA. Some countries that relied on natural gas have had to switch to coal as the main alternative for powering their electrical grids, due to the shipping constraints on liquid natural gas (LNG) through the Strait of Hormuz.

But in some cases, reactively reverting to cheaper and dirtier coal is happening in tandem with a proactive clean transition. Both Pakistan and the Philippines have increased their use of coal to offset some of the dependence on gas, but Pakistan's solar transition has been in the works for several years, with solar's slice of the electricity mix nearly tripling between 2023 and 2025, according to Ember.

Even as most of its LNG supply comes from Qatar, Pakistan's Power Minister Awais ‌Leghari was quick to point out how the country's uptake in renewables would cushion it from the disruptions in the Middle East, telling Reuters, "Pakistan is not expected to invest in any source of power that could put it at risk in terms of energy security."
Erica Downs, a senior research scholar at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University in New York, said electrification inevitably enhances energy security.
"What country doesn't want to be increasingly self-sufficient in energy production and supply?"

Montreal-based Northern Light Capital Partners led a study that showed that by March 30, a month after the start of the Iran war, more than 150 countries had announced they were investing in clean energy for energy security reasons.

"The U.S. administration's tariffs injected erratic volatility into clean energy supply chains," Joanna Klimczak, founder and CEO of Northern Light Capital Partners, told CBC News. "The war in Iran, meanwhile, has been a definitive accelerant for clean energy investment globally."
'A marathon, not a sprint'
The story of the renewable energy transition can't be told without highlighting China's role. It has been producing solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicles at a dizzying pace.

Early in his second term, Trump slapped massive tariffs on a variety of Chinese products, including solar panels. One result is that a lot of them were redirected to Africa, where they are helping countries such as Rwanda, Senegal, Ivory Coast and even oil-rich Nigeria end their reliance on fossil fuels like diesel.

"The cost of equipment went down when the trade war started. The Chinese were desperate to offload," Fawen Nyakudya, managing director of Zimbabwe-based PFN Solar Systems, told German media outlet DW.
Klimczak says that as a result of decades of investment in clean tech manufacturing, China has been able to accommodate global demand for renewable energy at a decisive moment.

Downs points out that unlike during the oil shocks in 1973 (due to the OPEC embargo), 1979 (the Iranian revolution) and 1990 (the first Iraq war), "there are technologies that exist today that give people alternatives to fossil fuels that they wouldn't have had in decades past."
They're not only available but, in most cases, are cheaper to deploy than traditional fossil fuels.

According to the International Renewable Energy Agency, since 2010, the installed costs of solar have declined by 87 per cent, onshore wind by 55 per cent and battery storage has fallen by 93 per cent.

Downs says it's "still a little early to tell" if Trump's trade and military exploits have had a lasting impact on the global energy transition. One key question is whether the price of oil went high enough "to force a more permanent shift to clean tech."
On Monday, the price of a barrel of Brent crude hit $109 US — the highest since May. But oil has yet to reach the lofty levels some analysts predicted earlier in the year.
"Oil didn't hit $200 [a barrel] — didn't hit $150," Downs said. "I've heard some people question, is it actually not a good thing, in the long term, that prices did not reach those sky-high levels?"
The energy transition is inevitable, Bond says, and moments like this accelerate the pace.

"This is a marathon, not a sprint. There is an ongoing shift from fossil fuels to alternatives that's been going on for a long time," he said. "And every time there's a shock like this, it just encourages people [to change] a little bit faster."

articles.title: Ferry June Aster fire death toll rises to 77 after survivor dies
articles.summary: A crew member of MV June Aster, who initially survived the Coron fire incident, has died on Tuesday afternoon, September 15.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 4:12pm
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) recovered 30 bodies from MV June Aster, which were brought to the Port of Borac, on September 12, 2026.
Photos courtesy of PCG
MANILA, Philippines — A crew member who initially survived the fire that swept through a passenger ferry in Coron, Palawan, died Tuesday afternoon, September 15, bringing the death toll to 77.

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) announced on Wednesday, September 16, that the crew member was declared dead by the Culion Sanitarium and General Hospital at around 11:34 a.m., where he was receiving treatment.
Earlier, authorities said the total number of survivors went up to 44 after the captain of the MV June Aster appeared before the PCG days after the incident.
However, with the crew member's death, the number of survivors went back to 43, while 12 people remain missing.
A total of 132 passengers were aboard the vessel when the fire broke out on September 9. Two people who were initially included in the ticket manifest had missed the trip.
Victims’ kin, survivors to receive aid

Meanwhile, the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), a government agency responsible for the country’s maritime sector, said the families of those who died, as well as the survivors, will receive assistance from the ship’s operator, Atienza Interisland Ferries, Inc.

MARINA Regional Office 4 Director Maximo Bañares Jr. said in an interview with dzMM on Wednesday that the MV June Aster has around P64 million worth of insurance that can be used to provide assistance to the victims.
Based on MARINA’s guidelines, survivors are entitled to claim at least P50,000 in assistance, while families of those who passed away are entitled to at least P200,000.
This assistance, according to Bañares, must be automatically granted to the claimants as long as proper documents to prove injuries and death are provided.
Families of those who died may also file for additional claims.

“'Yun pong P200,000 ay administrative rules lang po ng MARINA ‘yan. ‘Yung ibang mga apektado po ay maaaring pong mag-seek ng other remedies po para po madagdagan ‘yung claim nila kung gugustuhin nila,” Bañares said.
(The P200,000 is based only on the administrative rules of MARINA. Those who were affected may seek other remedies to increase their claims if they want.)

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Wednesday, September 16:

September 16, 2026
US bill sanctioning Russia could adversely impact India

India-US ties could come under pressure as the US lawmakers consider a Russia sanctions bill that would allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas. India, a major consumer of Russian energy, could be affected by the measure.

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in a 214-211 vote, media reports said. The House is expected to hold a final vote on Wednesday.
The bill, imposing sanctions on Russia's leadership, energy and defense sectors and "shadow fleet" accused of helping Moscow evade oil sanctions, was passed by the Senate last month.
If approved by the House, the bill would go to Trump to be signed into law.
The proposed tariffs seek toincrease economic pressure on Moscow by targeting countries that continue buying Russian energy.
India-US ties facing test

While India and Russia ties have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports, the same cannot be said of India-US relations under Prime Minister Narendra Modi as tensions mounted over New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil.
Last August, Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian imports over those purchases, on top of a 25% reciprocal tariff.
However, the additional Russia-related tariff was removed in February 2026, while the reciprocal tariff was reduced to 18% as part of a US-India trade framework.
However, the landmark bilateral trade agreement between the two countries remains in limbo, with no significant breakthrough.
